🪤 Biggest traps

  • Postpartum is 6 weeks. Mortality is 1 year.
  • Void first, then fundus.
  • Fundus pushed right or left = full bladder.
  • Lochia never goes backward.
  • Cold, not warm, for engorgement when not nursing. Never cold BEFORE feeding if nursing.
  • Breastfeeding is not contraception. No estrogen pills while nursing.
  • Chest pain is 911. Pad soaked in an hour is the provider (M-GILL).
  • Bonding one way, attachment two way.
  • Motherhood starts in pregnancy.
  • Tdap is for the baby's pertussis protection.

🩸 Day 2: Assessment, Uterus, and Lochia

Definitions first: maternal mortality, BUBBLE LE, involution, subinvolution, lochia, and REEDA.

🧠 The big idea

Postpartum is a bleeding watch plus a whole body reset.
Placenta delivered → hormones fall and the uterus must clamp down → Firm fundus and normal lochia mean it is working → Boggy fundus or heavy lochia means hemorrhage risk

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Postpartum is the first 6 weeks after childbirth. Maternal mortality counts deaths up to 1 year.
  2. BUBBLE LE: Breasts, Uterus, Bladder, Bowel, Lochia, Episiotomy (perineum), Lower extremities, Emotions.
  3. Fundal assessment: void first, then support the lower uterine segment. Look at position, tone, and location.
  4. Lochia goes rubra (dark red), serosa (pinkish-brown), alba (yellowish-white). Total about 200 to 500 mL over 3 to 6 weeks.
  5. REEDA: Redness, Edema, Ecchymosis, Discharge or Drainage, Approximation.

🎤 Postpartum basics

Marked 🎤 = said in her Day 2 lecture. Where the lecture and slides differ, this guide uses the lecture.

TopicWhat she said
Postpartum periodThe first 6 weeks after birth. Everything must return to normal, and it does not happen all at once.
Maternal mortalityDeaths from pregnancy or childbirth complications up to 1 year after birth. Goal: Healthy People 2030. Prenatal care and keeping postpartum appointments lower it.
Causes, in her order1) Obstetric hemorrhage (number one). 2) Hypertensive disorders. 3) Pregnancy-related infection. 4) Abortive outcomes (miscarriage, induced abortion). 5) Other OB causes. 6) Anesthesia complications, about 2%.
Vital signsEvery 15 minutes right after delivery, every 30 minutes after about an hour, then every 4 hours for the first 24 hours. Unit specific. Sicker clients are checked more often.
Three labsCBC (how much blood was lost). Rubella status (MMR or not). Rh status (RhoGAM or not).
RhoGAMMom Rh-negative and baby Rh-positive (the baby can be tested). Without it, mom makes antibodies that put future pregnancies in jeopardy.
VaccinesTdap (mostly for pertussis, to protect the baby), flu, and COVID. MMR if not rubella immune, then avoid pregnancy for 4 weeks.
🧠 Vital signs
15 - 30 - 4
Every 15 minutes right after delivery, every 30 minutes after about an hour, then every 4 hours for the first 24 hours.

🎤 Uterus, lochia, and perineum

Marked 🎤 = said in her Day 2 lecture. Where the lecture and slides differ, this guide uses the lecture.

TopicWhat she said
Want to findFundus firm, midline, and descending. Boggy means massage. Displaced right or left means a full bladder, which can cause atony, so have her void (straight cath only if she cannot).
Where it should beAt the umbilicus on delivery day, then down about 1 fingerbreadth (1 cm) a day for about 9 days, then it cannot be felt.
Not descending or coming upWorry about incomplete involution. Causes: retained placenta (pieces must be removed), full bladder, infection.
How to palpateVoid first. One hand supports the lower uterine segment (prevents inversion), the other finds the top. Check bleeding at the same time. Look at the perineum every time.
Cervix picturesA: never had a baby, pinpoint os. B: after childbirth, slit-like opening.
Lochia rubraDays 1 to 4 (she said 3 to 4). Dark red, small clots allowed, like a heavy period. Fleshy odor.
Lochia serosaDays 4 to 12. Flow decreases and thins. Pinkish-brown.
Lochia albaDay 12 to about 3 weeks. Creamy whitish, gradually disappears.
Lochia rulesIt must NEVER go backward (back to rubra after serosa or alba): she calls her OB, hemorrhage risk. Fishy odor means infection. A gush when she stands is normal because blood pools while lying down. A constant trickle is not.
Lochia as a windowLochia shows how the endometrium and the large placental site are healing.
REEDARedness, Edema, Ecchymosis, Discharge or Drainage, Approximation.
Lower extremitiesLooking for blood clots. Clotting factors stay high for about 2 weeks.
EmotionsHormones swing and she is tired. Ask about bonding and support.
🧠 Fundus
U at 0, minus 1 a day, gone by 9
Umbilicus on delivery day, down 1 cm (one fingerbreadth) a day, not palpable by about day 9.
🧠 Lochia
Red, Pink-brown, White
Rubra (ruby red) days 1 to 4. Serosa (serum, pink-brown) days 4 to 12. Alba (white) day 12 to 3 weeks. Never backward.
🧠 Deviated fundus
Right or left? Pee first
A full bladder pushes the uterus aside and makes it boggy. Empty the bladder, then massage if it is still boggy.

🧪 Say it first: Assessment, uterus, lochia

Say the answer out loud first. Then tap the question to check yourself.

What is the number one cause of postpartum complications and death?
Obstetric hemorrhage. Then hypertensive disorders, then infection.
How often are vitals taken after delivery?
Every 15 min, every 30 min after about an hour, then every 4 hours for 24 hours.
Why check the CBC, rubella status, and Rh status?
CBC: blood loss. Rubella: MMR. Rh: RhoGAM (mom negative, baby positive).
Why make sure the Tdap is current?
Mostly for pertussis, to protect the baby.
How long to avoid pregnancy after MMR?
4 weeks.
Where is the fundus on delivery day, and how does it move?
At the umbilicus, then down about 1 fingerbreadth (1 cm) a day until it cannot be felt around day 9.
The fundus is pushed to the right. What does it mean and what do you do?
A full bladder, which can cause atony. Have her void. Straight cath only if needed.
Why support the lower uterine segment?
To prevent uterine inversion.
Name 3 causes of a fundus that does not descend.
Retained placenta, distended bladder, infection.
Lochia stages, days, and colors?
Rubra days 1-4 dark red. Serosa days 4-12 pinkish-brown. Alba day 12 to 3 weeks creamy white.
Lochia goes back to bright red after serosa. What now?
She calls her OB. It should never go backward. Hemorrhage risk.
Is a gush of blood when she stands up an emergency?
No. Blood pools while lying down. A constant trickle would be a concern.
What does a fishy lochia odor mean?
Infection.
What are you looking for in the legs?
Blood clots (DVT).
What does the A picture of the cervix show? The B picture?
A: nulliparous pinpoint os. B: slit-like os after childbirth.
What does REEDA stand for?
Redness, Edema, Ecchymosis, Discharge or Drainage, Approximation.

🪤 Traps to dodge

⚠️ 6 weeks vs 1 yearPostpartum period = 6 weeks. Maternal mortality window = 1 year. Questions swap them.
⚠️ Lochia timingUse the main chart: rubra birth to 3 or 4 days, serosa 4 to 12 days, alba 12 days to 3 weeks. A second picture on her slides gives slightly different days (1 to 4, 5 to 9, 10 to 14). If both appear, go by color and flow: red heavy = rubra, pinkish-brown = serosa, yellowish-white scant = alba.
⚠️ Lochia must NOT go backwardHer lecture: lochia should never regress. Alba or serosa going back to rubra is concerning, so she calls her OB because it can signal a hemorrhage risk. The slides add that overactivity can bring rubra back, so teach rest, but the call still happens.
⚠️ Endometrium vs fundusEndometrial changes are assessed by lochia. Fundal height shows involution. Her slide question has "all of the above" as a trap.
⚠️ Void firstA full bladder pushes the uterus up and aside and makes it boggy. Always empty the bladder before judging the fundus.

📖 Definitions: assessment, uterus, lochia, perineum (51 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Say each meaning out loud, then check.

TermMeaning
Maternal mortalityDeath from complications of pregnancy or childbirth up to 1 year after birth.
Maternal mortality rateMaternal deaths per 100,000 births. Slide figures for 2023: 12.5 per 100,000 at 25 years or younger, 18.1 at ages 25 to 39, 59.8 at 40 years or older.
Healthy People 2030The national set of health goals named on her slide for preventing maternal death.
Leading causes of maternal death (slide pie chart)Obstetric hemorrhage 44%, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy 28%, pregnancy-related infections 10%, abortive outcomes 7%, other obstetric causes 7%, anesthetic complications 2%.
Postpartum periodThe first 6 weeks after childbirth. It includes physical changes plus social and emotional adaptation. Also called: Puerperium.
Postpartum assessment (overview)Vital signs, pain, breath and heart sounds, laboratory findings, and vaccination status, then breasts, uterus, bladder, bowel, lochia, episiotomy or lacerations or perineum or hemorrhoids, lower extremities, and emotions, bonding with the infant, fatigue, and psychosocial factors.
BUBBLE LEPostpartum head-to-toe memory aid: Breasts, Uterus, Bladder, Bowel, Lochia, Episiotomy (perineum), Lower extremities, Emotions. Also called: BUBBLE EE.
Uterine involutionThe return of the uterus to its nonpregnant state after birth. The nurse assesses the position, tone, and location of the fundus. The fundus is at the umbilicus after birth and drops about 1 fingerbreadth (1 cm) per day until it cannot be felt at about 9 days.
FundusThe top of the uterus. After birth it is assessed for position, tone, and location (height compared with the umbilicus).
Fundal assessment steps (slide)Instruct her to void first, then support the lower uterine segment while assessing the fundus.
Supporting the lower uterine segmentOne hand supports the lower uterus just above the symphysis pubis while the other hand assesses the fundus. Her slide lists it as a step of fundal assessment.
Firm fundusA well contracted uterus that feels like a firm ball. Expected after birth. Case study: firm, midline, at the level of the umbilicus.
Boggy uterusA soft, relaxed uterus. It most strongly suggests uterine atony and an increased risk of bleeding (case study question).
Uterine atonyFailure of the uterus to contract firmly after birth, leaving it boggy. It is on her Box 16.1 list of risk factors for postpartum hemorrhage.
SubinvolutionIncomplete involution of the uterus after birth.
Causes of subinvolutionRetained placental fragments, distended bladder, uterine myoma, and infection.
Complications of subinvolutionHemorrhage, pelvic peritonitis, salpingitis, and abscess formation.
Endometrial changesAssessed by examining the lochia. The appearance and amount of lochia show the progress of endometrial shedding and regeneration.
LochiaThe vaginal discharge after birth as the uterus sheds its lining. Total volume is about 200 to 500 mL and it can last 3 to 6 weeks. Lochia can last up to 5 weeks (patient education slide).
Lochia rubraDark red blood from the birth until 3 to 4 days postpartum. Flow like a heavy menstrual period, may have small clots, and the odor is fleshy like menstrual blood.
Lochia serosaPinkish-brownish discharge from about 4 to 12 days postpartum (about 2 weeks). The flow is a moderate to small amount.
Lochia albaYellowish-white discharge from about 12 days to 3 weeks postpartum. Scant, creamy, and whitish, gradually disappearing.
Lochia that goes backwardLochia should not progress backward. A return to rubra after serosa or alba needs a call to the OB because of hemorrhage risk. Her slide adds that overactivity or stress may cause it.
Scant lochiaBlood only on the tissue when wiped, or a stain on the peri pad less than 1 inch (2.5 cm).
Light lochiaA stain on the peri pad less than 4 inches (10 cm).
Moderate lochiaA stain on the peri pad less than 6 inches (15.2 cm).
Heavy lochiaA peri pad saturated within 1 hour.
REEDAScale for assessing perineum healing: Redness, Edema, Ecchymosis, Discharge or Drainage, Approximation.
Redness (REEDA)Erythema at the perineal repair or episiotomy site.
Edema (REEDA)Swelling of the perineal tissue.
Ecchymosis (REEDA)Bruising of the perineal tissue.
Discharge or drainage (REEDA)Fluid draining from the perineal wound. The nurse notes the amount and type.
Approximation (REEDA)How well the edges of the repair line up and stay together.
Reproductive system nursing focusUterine involution (position, tone, location of the fundus), the endometrium (lochia color, amount, odor), the vagina and perineum (REEDA), and breast care and assessment.
Postpartum vital sign schedule (lecture)Every 15 minutes right after delivery, every 30 minutes after about an hour, then every 4 hours for the first 24 hours. It is unit specific, and sicker clients are checked more often.
Postpartum labs (lecture)CBC to see how much blood was lost, rubella status to decide on MMR, and Rh status to decide on RhoGAM.
Tdap postpartum (lecture)Make sure the tetanus shot is current. It is mainly for pertussis (whooping cough), to protect the baby. Flu and COVID vaccines are also recommended.
Fundal progression (lecture)At the umbilicus on the day of delivery, then down about 1 fingerbreadth (1 cm) per day for about 9 days, until it cannot be felt.
Fundus not descendingA fundus that is not descending, or is coming back up, raises worry about incomplete involution (subinvolution).
Deviated fundus (lecture)A fundus displaced to the right or left means a full bladder is pressing on it. A full bladder can cause uterine atony. Have her void, and straight cath only if needed.
Uterine inversionThe uterus turns inside out. Supporting the lower uterine segment with one hand below and one on top during fundal assessment helps prevent it.
Retained placenta (lecture)A cause of subinvolution. The retained pieces must be removed.
Lochia gush on standingBlood pools while lying down and gushes out when she stands. This is normal. A constant trickle is not.
Fishy lochia odorWorry about infection. Normal lochia has a fleshy odor like menstrual blood.
Nulliparous cervix (picture A)The cervical os of a woman who has never had a baby is a small pinpoint.
Parous cervix (picture B)After childbirth the os becomes a slit-like opening.
Perineum check with every fundal checkWhenever the fundus is assessed, also look at the perineum to watch the repair and the bleeding.
Lower extremity assessmentLooks for blood clots (DVT). Clotting factors are high in pregnancy and take about 2 weeks to return to normal.
Obstetric hemorrhageThe number one cause of postpartum complications and maternal death. Hypertensive disorders come second.
Abortive outcomesMiscarriage and induced abortion. Listed among the causes of pregnancy-related death.
Fundus displaced right or leftSuggests a full bladder pushing the uterus aside. Have her void before judging the fundus.

🩺 Lecture vs slides, and what is still unconfirmed

  • Lochia timing: her lecture matches the main chart (rubra days 1 to 4, serosa 4 to 12, alba 12 days to 3 weeks). The second slide picture is shorter (1 to 4, 5 to 9, 10 to 14), so this guide uses the lecture.
  • Lochia length: slides say 3 to 6 weeks. In lecture she said about 5 weeks, and told Maria 5 to 6. Know "up to about 5 to 6 weeks."
  • Lochia going backward: she said it should NOT, and the client calls her OB. An earlier version of this guide said it was not an emergency. That was changed to match the lecture.
  • Cervix pictures: now confirmed in lecture (A is the pinpoint os of a woman who has not had a baby, B is the slit after childbirth).
  • Pad amount chart (scant, light, moderate, heavy): from her slides only, not repeated in lecture.
  • Vital sign schedule: she said it is unit specific. 15, 30, 4 is her example.

🍼 Day 2: Breasts and Body Systems

Definitions first: engorgement, suppressing lactation, and each body system after birth.

🧠 The big idea

Every body system reverses pregnancy in its own way, and each has one risk to watch.
Blood: low H&H, high WBC, orthostatic hypotension → Lungs: pulmonary edema risks → Bladder: distention and UTI → Hormones: fall, then prolactin by suckling → Muscles: diastasis, Kegels → Gut: constipation and hemorrhoids

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Not breastfeeding: cool compresses (15 minutes on, 15 minutes off per her lecture), cold cabbage leaves, supportive bra, no stimulation.
  2. EBL 200 to 500 mL for vaginal birth. H&H low, WBC high. BP and RR decrease slightly, temperature increases slightly.
  3. Rubella vaccine if nonimmune, then avoid pregnancy 4 weeks. Rho(D) immune globulin for Rh-negative mom, Rh-positive baby, Coombs negative.
  4. Void every 3 to 4 hours. Fluid shift 6 to 8 liters, diuresis up to 3000 mL/day in the first 2 weeks.
  5. Menses return 10 to 12 weeks if not nursing, 4 to 5 months or longer if nursing. Ovulation can come first.

🎤 Breast care

Marked 🎤 = said in her Day 2 lecture. Where the lecture and slides differ, this guide uses the lecture.

TopicWhat she said
HormonesPlacenta delivered: estrogen and progesterone fall. Prolactin makes the milk. Oxytocin lets it down (letdown reflex). Infant suckling releases both, so it is a positive feedback system: more suckling, more milk.
Milk timelineThick colostrum first. Mature milk comes in about 4 to 5 days after birth. Engorgement is common around days 3 to 5.
FeedingOn demand, whenever the baby acts hungry, about 8 to 12 times in 24 hours. Alternate the starting breast (start on the one offered last). Drink enough fluids.
ATI likes thisWash hands before breastfeeding. Well-fitted bra with NO underwire (it clogs milk ducts).
Cracked nipplesCheck for a deep latch. Use lanolin. Rub a little breast milk on the nipple and let it dry.
Engorgement, breastfeedingEmpty often. Warm shower or warm compress BEFORE feeding. Cold between or after feeding. Never cold before feeding, because too much cold can dry up the milk.
Not breastfeeding (about 30%)Support her choice. Supportive well-fitted bra for the first 72 hours. Cool compresses 15 minutes on and 15 off. Fresh cold cabbage leaves in the bra. Avoid ANY breast stimulation, even a warm shower running on the breasts.
🧠 Breast care
Nursing: warm before, cold after. Not nursing: cold only, no touch
Warmth before a feed helps milk flow. Cold after eases swelling. If she is not nursing, warmth and touch make more milk, so use cold only.

🎤 Body systems

Marked 🎤 = said in her Day 2 lecture. Where the lecture and slides differ, this guide uses the lecture.

TopicWhat she said
CardiovascularBlood loss 200 to 500 mL. BP slightly low. Main risk: orthostatic hypotension and a fall. Iron if she was anemic. Clotting factors return to normal in about 2 weeks.
Early ambulationVaginal birth: up in a couple of hours. Cesarean: 12 to 24 hours, per facility. SCDs while in bed. No crossing legs.
Red flagsExcessive hypotension or tachycardia means worry about excessive blood loss and shock.
Temperature and chillsRR may decrease and temperature may rise slightly. Chills with a normal temperature: warm blanket. Chills with a high temperature: possible infection, tell the provider.
RespiratoryReturns to normal by the end of the postpartum period. Check RR and breath sounds. Pulmonary edema risks: oxytocin with large IV fluids, terbutaline, magnesium sulfate with preeclampsia, bedrest.
ImmuneRubella immune? If not, MMR. Keep Tdap, flu, and COVID current to protect the baby. Rh isoimmunization: RhoGAM for an Rh-negative mom with an Rh-positive baby.
UrinaryStress incontinence and hard to void (large fluids, epidural, urethral edema). High UTI risk. Void at least every 4 hours and before any fundal check. Pelvic floor PT if it lasts.
Fluid shiftDiuresis from falling estrogen, especially in the first 12 hours. Up to about 3,000 mL of urine, and it can go for the first 2 weeks (uncommon).
EndocrineEstrogen, progesterone, and prolactin fall. Prolactin rises in a nursing mother. Insulin sensitivity returns to normal (slower if obese). With gestational diabetes only, insulin needs drop significantly.
Lochia and mensesLochia can last about 5 weeks. Menses return in about 10 to 12 weeks. The first cycle is often without ovulation, but she can still ovulate. Exclusively breastfeeding delays it, to around 6 months.
Muscular and nervousSore. Check that sensation returns after an epidural. Headache can occur. Promote rest and sleep. Diastasis recti resolves on its own in 6 to 8 weeks. If not, PT or surgery.
GIConstipation: less motility from progesterone, less activity, dehydration, fear of pain. Give stool softeners, fiber, and fluids. Hemorrhoids: Tucks pads and sitz baths, usually slowly resolve. Appetite is up.
WeightAbout 11 to 12 lb lost at delivery (baby, blood, fluid), 5 to 8 lb more from diuresis. Most are back to pre-pregnancy weight around 6 months.
🧠 Pulmonary edema
Oxytocin, Terbutaline, Magnesium, plus fluids and bedrest
Large IV fluids with oxytocin, terbutaline, magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia, and bedrest all raise the risk. Listen to breath sounds.
🧠 Weight
11 to 12, then 5 to 8
11 to 12 lb at delivery, 5 to 8 lb from diuresis, back to normal by about 6 months.

🧪 Say it first: Breasts and body systems

Say the answer out loud first. Then tap the question to check yourself.

Which hormone lets milk down? Which makes it?
Oxytocin lets it down. Prolactin makes it. Suckling releases both.
When does milk come in?
About 4 to 5 days after birth. Colostrum comes first.
How often does a breastfed baby feed?
On demand, 8 to 12 times in 24 hours.
Which breast does she start on?
Alternate. Start on the breast offered last.
Which bra for breastfeeding?
Well fitted, no underwire.
What helps cracked nipples?
Deep latch, lanolin, breast milk rubbed on and air dried.
Nursing mother is engorged: warm or cold?
Warm before feeds, cold after. Never cold before feeding.
Not breastfeeding and engorged: what do you do?
Supportive bra for 72 hours, cool compresses 15 on and 15 off, cold cabbage leaves, no stimulation.
Why is orthostatic hypotension a risk?
Blood loss of 200 to 500 mL. She could fall.
What do excessive hypotension and tachycardia suggest?
Excessive blood loss and shock.
Chills with a normal temperature?
Warm blanket.
Name 3 things that raise pulmonary edema risk.
Oxytocin with large IV fluids, terbutaline, magnesium sulfate. Also preeclampsia and bedrest.
Who gets RhoGAM?
Rh-negative mom with an Rh-positive baby.
How often does she void and why?
At least every 4 hours and before fundal checks. A full bladder displaces the uterus and UTI risk is high.
What happens to insulin needs after gestational diabetes?
They drop significantly.
What is the plan for diastasis recti?
Usually resolves in 6 to 8 weeks. PT or surgery if it does not.
How much weight is lost, and by when is she back to normal?
11 to 12 lb at delivery plus 5 to 8 lb from diuresis. Normal around 6 months.

🪤 Traps to dodge

⚠️ Engorgement without nursingWarm showers, nipple stimulation, and expressing milk all make MORE milk. The answer is cold.
⚠️ Breastfeeding is not contraceptionOvulation can come before the first period.
⚠️ Rho(D) immune globulinNeeds all three: Rh-negative mother, Rh-positive baby, Coombs negative. A positive Coombs means she already has antibodies.
⚠️ TemperatureA slight rise in the first 24 hours is normal. 100.4 F or higher is a call-the-provider sign.
⚠️ Large urine outputDiuresis up to 3000 mL/day is expected in the first 2 weeks. Do not mistake it for kidney or diabetes problems.

📖 Definitions: breasts and body systems (56 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Say each meaning out loud, then check.

TermMeaning
Breast care and assessmentAssess the breasts and teach breastfeeding and non-breastfeeding patients how to care for them.
EngorgementSwollen, inflamed, painful breasts with lactation. The infant has difficulty grasping the nipple, which can disrupt breastfeeding (Figure 15.4).
Suppressing lactationMilk stops eventually when there is no stimulus (no infant suckling or pumping). Cool compresses (15 minutes on, 15 minutes off per her lecture) and cold cabbage leaves ease engorgement.
Cool compresses for engorgementApplied 15 minutes on and 15 minutes off (her lecture) to ease engorgement in a woman who is not breastfeeding.
Cold cabbage leavesA comfort measure for engorgement listed on her slide for suppressing lactation.
Percent who do not breastfeedAround 30% of mothers will not breastfeed.
Estimated blood loss (EBL)Average 200 to 500 mL after a vaginal birth.
Orthostatic hypotensionA drop in blood pressure when she sits or stands up. She is at risk right after birth.
Expected postpartum labsH&H (hemoglobin and hematocrit) low and WBCs high.
Postpartum vital signsBP decreases slightly, RR decreases, temperature increases slightly, and there is an immediate weight loss.
Slight temperature rise (first 24 hours)A slight elevation in temperature during the first 24 hours postpartum is considered normal (her slide question, answer true).
Respiratory system postpartumReturns to the pre-pregnancy state by the end of the postpartum period. Breath sounds are assessed after birth.
Risk factors for pulmonary edemaOxytocin, large amounts of IV fluids, tocolytics, multiple birth, infection or preeclampsia, and bedrest.
Immune system postpartumSuppressed during pregnancy and returns to normal in the postpartum period.
Postpartum rubella vaccinationGiven to a woman who is rubella-nonimmune. She must prevent pregnancy for 4 weeks after the immunization.
Rho(D) immune globulinGiven to an Rh-negative woman who gave birth to an Rh-positive baby, when she is Coombs negative. Prevents Rh isoimmunization. Brand name: RhoGAM.
Rh isoimmunizationThe mother forming antibodies against Rh-positive blood. Prevented with Rho(D) immune globulin.
Coombs negativeHer antibody screen shows no Rh antibodies yet, so Rho(D) immune globulin can still prevent them.
Urinary risks postpartumBladder distention, urinary incontinence, an increased risk of UTI, and cystitis.
Urinary nursing actionsEncourage voiding every 3 to 4 hours and assess the volume excreted and for retention.
Fluid shiftFluid moves from the extravascular to the intravascular space after birth, about 6 to 8 liters.
Postpartum diuresisExcess pregnancy sodium and fluid are removed through inhibited aldosterone, angiotensin II, and vasopressin. Diuresis occurs during the first 2 weeks postpartum, with urine output up to 3000 mL/day.
Endocrine changes after birthAfter the placenta is delivered, estrogen, progesterone, and prolactin levels decrease. In breastfeeding women, prolactin increases in response to infant suckling.
DiaphoresisHeavy sweating after birth. It is an expected endocrine change.
Insulin sensitivity postpartumReturns in days, or in weeks if the woman is obese.
Return of menses10 to 12 weeks in nonlactating women. 4 to 5 months, and as much as 24 months, in lactating mothers.
Ovulation without mensesOvulation can occur before the first period returns, so she can become pregnant before she sees a period.
Diastasis recti abdominisSeparation of the rectus abdominis muscles along the linea alba. The nurse assesses for it in the muscular system.
Muscular and nervous nursing actionsAssess for diastasis recti abdominis, relieve muscle soreness, assess for return of sensation, headache, and fatigue, promote rest and sleep, and perform nursing actions.
Kegel exercisesSqueeze and lift the pelvic floor muscles (as if stopping urine or gas), hold 5 seconds, relax 5 seconds, repeat 5 times. They strengthen the pelvic floor.
Gastrointestinal changes postpartumConstipation, hemorrhoids, increased appetite, and weight loss. Encourage fluids and food.
Letdown reflexThe release of milk triggered by oxytocin. Infant suckling causes prolactin and oxytocin release.
Milk production hormonesAfter the placenta is delivered, estrogen and progesterone fall. Prolactin makes the milk and oxytocin causes letdown. Suckling is a positive feedback loop: more suckling, more milk.
ColostrumThe thick first milk. Mature creamy milk comes in about 4 to 5 days after delivery.
Breastfeeding on demandFeed whenever the baby acts hungry, about 8 to 12 times in 24 hours. Start each feeding on the breast offered last time.
Breastfeeding hand hygieneWash hands before breastfeeding to help prevent infection. ATI likes to ask about it.
Bra for a breastfeeding motherA well-fitted bra with no underwire. Underwire can cause clogged milk ducts.
Cracked nipples careCheck the latch for a deep latch, use lanolin cream, and express breast milk onto the nipples and let it dry.
Engorgement care when breastfeedingFrequent emptying, warm shower or warm compress before feeding, and cold between or after feedings. Never use cold before feeding because too much cold can dry up the milk supply.
Bra for a mother who is not breastfeedingA well-fitted supportive bra for the first 72 hours, and no breast stimulation, including warm showers running over the breasts.
Early ambulationVaginal birth clients are usually up within a couple of hours. Cesarean birth clients are up in about 12 to 24 hours, per facility policy.
SCDs and leg careSequential compression devices on while she is not up, and do not cross the legs. This keeps blood moving and prevents clots.
Excessive hypotension or tachycardia (postpartum)Worry about excessive blood loss and shock. A slightly low BP alone is expected.
Chills after birthWith a normal temperature, give a warm blanket. Fever with chills raises worry about infection, so notify the provider.
Meds that raise pulmonary edema riskOxytocin, terbutaline, and magnesium sulfate, along with large IV fluid volumes, preeclampsia, and bedrest.
Why Rh isoimmunization mattersThe mother makes antibodies against the baby's Rh-positive blood, which can put future pregnancies in jeopardy.
Stress incontinence postpartumLeaking urine with pressure. Epidural anesthesia, large fluid volumes, and urethral edema make voiding harder. Pelvic floor physical therapy helps if it lasts.
Diastasis recti courseUsually resolves on its own in about 6 to 8 weeks. If it does not, physical therapy or surgery may be needed.
Constipation causes postpartumDecreased GI motility from progesterone, less activity, dehydration or fluid loss, and fear of a bowel movement from lacerations or hemorrhoids. Give stool softeners, fiber, and fluids.
Hemorrhoid comfort measuresTucks pads and sitz baths. They usually resolve slowly on their own but can stay painful.
Postpartum weight lossAbout 11 to 12 lb at delivery (baby, blood, fluid), then about 5 to 8 lb more from diuresis. Most women are at pre-pregnancy weight by about 6 months.
Gestational diabetes postpartumInsulin needs drop significantly. If it was only gestational diabetes, she usually does not need insulin after birth.
Orthostatic hypotension (postpartum)A drop in blood pressure on standing. Risk after birth from blood loss. Check BP, sit her on the side of the bed to dangle, then help her stand.
DiuresisIncreased urine output after birth from falling estrogen. Up to about 3,000 mL a day, mostly in the first 12 hours, and uncommonly for up to 2 weeks.
First postpartum cycleOften without ovulation, but she can still ovulate. Menses return in about 10 to 12 weeks if not breastfeeding.
LanolinA breast cream used for cracked, sore nipples.

🍼 Breasts: lactating vs not

Not breastfeeding (about 30%)Milk stops eventually without suckling or pumping. Cool compresses 15 minutes on, 15 minutes off (lecture). Cold cabbage leaves

🧘 Kegel exercises (her picture)

StepWhat to do
1Lie down with knees slightly apart (or stand or sit)
2Tense the pelvic floor starting at the anus, as if stopping gas
3Tense around the vagina, as if stopping urine
4Squeeze both areas and lift toward the belly button
5Hold 5 seconds, relax 5 seconds
6Repeat 5 times
🧠 Systems cheat
Cool for non-nursers. Slow for orthostatics. Q 3 to 4 hours for the bladder.
Three actions cover most system questions: cool measures when not nursing, slow position changes after birth, and voiding every 3 to 4 hours.
🩺 Think like a nurseWhen you see "not breastfeeding", think cold and no stimulation. When you see "Rh-negative mom", check the baby's type and her Coombs before giving Rho(D) immune globulin.

🩺 Lecture vs slides, and what is still unconfirmed

  • Cool compresses: lecture says 15 minutes on and 15 minutes off. Her slide prints 15 on and 45 off. This guide uses the lecture, and both mean a short application with a rest.
  • Voiding: lecture says at least every 4 hours. Slides say every 3 to 4 hours. Never go longer than 4.
  • Menses: lecture and slide agree on about 10 to 12 weeks. The slide gives 4 to 5 months or longer if nursing. She said around 6 months if exclusively breastfeeding. The transcript also contains a "7 to 9 months" line that looks like a transcription error, so it is not used.
  • Lochia in this tab: up to about 5 weeks (see the first Day 2 tab).
  • Rho(D) immune globulin timing (usually within 72 hours) and the Coombs test are from the slides and standard teaching. She did not give a time in lecture.
  • Dehydration and diuresis: up to about 3,000 mL and up to 2 weeks (uncommon), as she said.

🏠 Day 2: Nursing Management and Discharge

Definitions first: nursing management, nutrition, sex and contraception, Box 16.1 risks, and POST BIRTH.

🧠 The big idea

Discharge teaching is the nurse's last chance to prevent a readmission or a death.
Teach recovery (food, rest, sex, contraception) → Teach warning signs (911 vs call the provider) → Screen mood (EPDS before discharge and again at 10 days) → Know who is high risk (Box 16.1)

⭐ Know these cold

  1. EPDS before discharge, then again at home at about 10 days. A score over 10 means call the OB. Many women skip follow-up.
  2. Nonlactating 1,800 to 2,200 kcal. Lactating add about 450 to 500 kcal. Prenatal vitamins until 6 weeks. High protein diet.
  3. Sex: when lochia stops, perineum is healed, and she is ready, with contraception first. Breastfeeding is NOT contraception.
  4. 911: chest pain, trouble breathing, seizures, thoughts of hurting self or baby.
  5. Provider: pad soaked in 1 hour or egg-size clot, incision not healing, red warm painful leg, 100.4 F or higher, headache not relieved or with vision changes.

🎤 Nursing management

Marked 🎤 = said in her Day 2 lecture. Where the lecture and slides differ, this guide uses the lecture.

TopicWhat she said
Culturally congruent careAsk what she wants. It can be as simple as warm or cold fluids.
ComfortIce the perineum for about the first 24 hours only (longer delays healing). Heating pad for comfort. Dermoplast spray, Tucks pads, witch hazel. Sitz baths.
Pain medicineStart with ibuprofen and acetaminophen. For severe lacerations, hemorrhoids, or a cesarean, the provider may order something stronger like Norco (hydrocodone and acetaminophen). Encourage her to take it so she can do more.
EliminationHelp with bowel and bladder. Stool softeners, good diet, fluids.
ActivityEarly ambulation and frequent rest periods. Rest when the baby rests. Kegels: tense, then relax the pelvic floor.
Safe first walkCheck BP, sit on the side of the bed to dangle, help her stand, walk WITH her. Never alone, especially the first times.
Feeding choiceSupport breast, bottle, or pumping. Teach breast care and suppression. Teach about postpartum blues.
NutritionNonlactating 1,800 to 2,200 kcal a day. Lactating add 450 to 500 kcal. High protein for tissue repair. Iron if needed. Prenatal vitamins at least 6 weeks.
EPDSBefore discharge, then a second copy at home at about 10 days. A score over 10 means call the OB (high risk for postpartum depression). She may need referrals, family support, or a counselor.
Follow-upSet appointments BEFORE discharge. Newborn within 1 to 2 days of discharge. Mom at least 6 weeks. Many skip their own visit and keep only the pediatrician.

🎤 Sex, contraception, smoking

Marked 🎤 = said in her Day 2 lecture. Where the lecture and slides differ, this guide uses the lecture.

TopicWhat she said
Resuming sexWhen lochia stops (uterus healed, usually around 6 weeks), she is cleared by her OB, and she is physically AND emotionally ready.
Contraception firstHave it in place before sex resumes. It is usually discussed in the hospital and documented before discharge.
BreastfeedingNOT contraception. Very unreliable. Ovulation return is unknown.
If nursing and wants hormonesNO combined (estrogen) pills. Progestin-only is preferred: the mini pill, Depo-Provera injection, or an IUD (easier to place postpartum).
SmokingMany who quit in pregnancy relapse. Encourage her to stay quit. Teach secondhand smoke risks, including a higher SIDS risk.

🎤 Contraception names (generic and brand)

MethodGenericBrand examplesEstrogen?
Mini pillNorethindroneCamila, ErrinNo. OK while nursing
InjectionMedroxyprogesteroneDepo-ProveraNo. OK while nursing
Hormonal IUDLevonorgestrelMirena, Kyleena, Liletta, SkylaNo. OK while nursing
Copper IUDCopper (no hormone)ParaGardNo. OK while nursing
ImplantEtonogestrelNexplanonNo. OK while nursing
Combined pillEstrogen plus progestinMany brandsYES. Avoid while nursing

In lecture she named the mini pill, Depo-Provera, and an IUD, and said no combined oral contraceptives. The implant, copper IUD, and brand names are standard teaching and are not from her lecture.

🎤 POST BIRTH, her version

Call 911 (POST)Call the provider (M-GILL)
Pain in the chestMassive bleeding: a pad an hour or an egg-size clot
Obstructed breathing or shortness of breathGrowing incision problem: red, warm, or painful
SeizuresInfection: temperature 100.4 F or higher
Thoughts of hurting yourself or the babyLeg pain or swelling
Lingering headache or vision changes

Right upper quadrant pain is not on the list, but she said it is still a red flag (gallbladder, liver). A slight temperature rise in the first 24 hours can be normal. Worry about chills or a temperature that continues past 24 hours.

🧠 911
POST
Pain in chest, Obstructed breathing, Seizures, Thoughts of hurting self or baby.
🧠 Provider
M-GILL
Massive bleeding, Growing incision, Infection, Leg pain or swelling, Lingering headache or vision changes.
🧠 Nursing mom birth control
M-D-I: Mini pill, Depo, IUD
No estrogen. Progestin-only choices. An IUD is easy to place postpartum.
🧠 Follow-up clock
Baby 1 to 2 days. EPDS day 10. Mom 6 weeks
Set every appointment before discharge. Many mothers skip their own.

🧪 Say it first: Management and discharge

Say the answer out loud first. Then tap the question to check yourself.

How long do you ice the perineum?
About the first 24 hours. Longer delays healing.
Name the perineal comfort products she listed.
Dermoplast spray, Tucks pads, witch hazel, sitz bath, heating pad.
Which pain medicines come first?
Ibuprofen and acetaminophen. Stronger (Norco) for severe lacerations, hemorrhoids, or cesarean.
How do you get her up safely the first time?
Check BP, sit and dangle, stand, walk with her. Not alone.
How many calories do nonlactating and lactating clients need?
1,800 to 2,200 a day. Lactating add 450 to 500.
How long do prenatal vitamins continue?
At least 6 weeks.
When is the EPDS done and what score matters?
At discharge and about 10 days. Over 10 means call the OB.
When are follow-up visits?
Newborn within 1-2 days of discharge. Mother about 6 weeks. Schedule before discharge.
When can she resume sex?
Lochia stopped (about 6 weeks), cleared by the OB, emotionally ready. Contraception first.
Is breastfeeding contraception?
No. It is unreliable.
Which birth control does a nursing mom avoid?
Combined (estrogen) pills.
Which are preferred?
Progestin-only: mini pill, Depo-Provera, IUD.
Say POST.
Pain in chest, Obstructed breathing, Seizures, Thoughts of hurting self or baby. Call 911.
Say M-GILL.
Massive bleeding, Growing incision, Infection (100.4 F), Leg pain or swelling, Lingering headache or vision changes. Call the provider.
Is right upper quadrant pain on POST BIRTH?
No, but it is still a red flag (gallbladder or liver).
What does secondhand smoke add for the baby?
A higher SIDS risk.

🪤 Traps to dodge

⚠️ 911 vs providerChest pain, breathing trouble, seizures, and thoughts of harm are 911. Everything else on the list is a call to the provider.
⚠️ Infection vs hemorrhage risksInfection: long (labor or ruptured membranes over 24 hours), catheter, diabetes, anemia, manual removal. Hemorrhage: too fast (under 3 hours), too long (third stage over 30 minutes), too stretched, tissue left, atony.
⚠️ Pad soaked in an hourOn POST BIRTH it means call the provider. In the hospital, treat it as hemorrhage right away.
⚠️ Breastfeeding is not birth controlHave contraception on board before sex resumes.

📖 Definitions: nursing management and discharge (38 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Say each meaning out loud, then check.

TermMeaning
Nursing management in the postpartum periodCulturally optimal care, promoting comfort, assisting with elimination, promoting activity, rest, and exercise, assisting with self-care, ensuring safety, counseling about sexuality and contraception, promoting nutrition, supporting the choice of newborn feeding method, teaching about breast care, and teaching about postpartum blues.
Postpartum follow-up visitA comprehensive assessment and depression screening within 4 to 6 weeks. Many women do not have postpartum follow-up.
Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)The screening tool for postpartum depression. Done before discharge, again at about 10 days at home, and at the follow-up visit. A score over 10 means call the OB.
Discharge teaching topicsNutrition and fluids, physical activity and exercise, rest and comfort, sexual activity, family planning and contraception, smoking cessation and relapse prevention, and warning signs.
Nonlactating calorie goal1,800 to 2,200 kcal per day.
Lactating calorie goalIncrease calories by about 450 to 500 kcal per day.
Postpartum dietA well-balanced diet high in protein for tissue repair. Iron supplementation may be required.
Prenatal vitamins postpartumRecommended until 6 weeks postpartum.
Activity and rest teachingKegel exercises, rest for healing and lactation, rest when the baby rests, and take medications as ordered (iron, vitamins, pain medications).
Resuming sexual activityDiscuss with the provider. General guideline: when lochia stops, the perineum is healed, and she is physically and emotionally ready.
Contraception before sexHave contraception in place before sex resumes. Breastfeeding is NOT contraception.
Smoking cessation teachingEncourage women who quit during pregnancy to continue to abstain, warn about secondhand smoke, and know that most who quit will relapse after delivery.
Risk factors for postpartum infectionOperative procedure (cesarean, vacuum), history of diabetes including gestational diabetes, prolonged labor over 24 hours, indwelling urinary catheter, anemia (hemoglobin under 10.5), multiple vaginal exams, prolonged rupture of membranes over 24 hours, manual extraction of placenta, and compromised immune system (HIV positive).
Risk factors for postpartum hemorrhagePrecipitous labor (under 3 hours), uterine atony, placenta previa or abruptio placentae, labor induction or augmentation, operative procedures, retained placental fragments, prolonged third stage (over 30 minutes), multiparity with more than three closely spaced births, and uterine overdistention (large infant, twins, hydramnios).
Precipitous labor (Box 16.1)Labor of less than 3 hours. A risk factor for postpartum hemorrhage.
Prolonged labor (Box 16.1)Labor of more than 24 hours. A risk factor for postpartum infection.
Prolonged third stage (Box 16.1)A third stage of labor of more than 30 minutes. A risk factor for postpartum hemorrhage.
Uterine overdistentionOverstretching of the uterus by a large infant, twins, or hydramnios. A risk factor for postpartum hemorrhage.
AWHONN POST BIRTHThe 2018 AWHONN discharge teaching project that tells women when to call 911 and when to call the provider.
Call 911 (POST BIRTH)Pain in the chest, obstructed breathing or shortness of breath, seizures, and thoughts of hurting yourself or the baby.
Call the provider (POST BIRTH, M-GILL)Bleeding that soaks through one pad per hour or a clot the size of an egg, an incision that is not healing, a red or swollen leg that is warm or painful to the touch, a temperature of 100.4 F or higher, and a headache that does not improve with medication or comes with vision changes.
Ice to the perineumIce for about the first 24 hours only. Longer than 24 hours can delay healing.
Perineal comfort productsDermoplast spray, Tucks pads, and witch hazel. Heat from a heating pad can also be used for comfort.
First-line postpartum pain medicinesIbuprofen (Motrin, Advil) and acetaminophen (Tylenol) first. Stronger options such as hydrocodone and acetaminophen (Norco) are for severe lacerations, hemorrhoids, or cesarean birth.
Safe first ambulationCheck BP, sit her on the side of the bed to dangle, then help her stand and walk with her. Never let her walk alone the first times because of orthostatic hypotension.
EPDS schedule (lecture)Before discharge, then a second copy at about 10 days postpartum at home. A score over 10 means call the OB.
Postpartum follow-up (lecture)Set the appointments before discharge. Newborn follow-up within 1 to 2 days of discharge. Mother at least 6 weeks. Many keep the pediatrician visit and skip the OB visit.
Contraception while breastfeedingBreastfeeding is unreliable. Avoid combined (estrogen) oral contraceptives. Progestin-only options are preferred: the mini pill, Depo-Provera injection, and an IUD, which is easy to place postpartum.
Combined oral contraceptivesPills with estrogen and progestin. Avoided while breastfeeding.
POST (call 911)Pain in the chest, Obstructed breathing or shortness of breath, Seizures, Thoughts of hurting yourself or the baby.
M-GILL (call the provider)Massive bleeding (pad an hour or egg-size clot), Growing incision problem, Infection (temperature 100.4 F or higher), Leg pain or swelling, Lingering headache or vision changes.
Temperature concern (lecture)A slight rise in the first 24 hours can come from dehydration or fluid loss. Worry if it comes with chills or continues past the first 24 hours.
Secondhand smoke riskChildren exposed are at higher risk of SIDS. Teach it because most who quit during pregnancy relapse after delivery.
Mini pillA progestin-only birth control pill (norethindrone). Preferred over combined pills while breastfeeding.
Depo-ProveraA progestin injection (medroxyprogesterone). An option for the breastfeeding mother.
IUD postpartumAn intrauterine device. It is easier to place postpartum and has no estrogen.
Rest with the babyTeach her to rest when the baby sleeps so she can heal and her milk can come in.
Pain medicine teachingPain medicine helps her do more of her usual activity, so encourage her to take it as ordered.

🩺 Lecture vs slides, and what is still unconfirmed

  • Brand names and the implant or copper IUD: standard teaching, not from lecture.
  • Box 16.1: prints hemoglobin under 10.5 mg/dL. Hemoglobin is measured in g/dL, so the unit looks like a typo.

👪 Day 2: Parenthood, Bonding, and Blues

Definitions first: motherhood stages, special parent groups, bonding vs attachment, infant states, and postpartum blues.

🧠 The big idea

Becoming a parent is a process, and the nurse supports it.
Motherhood moves through four stages → Fathers, teens, and same-sex parents adapt differently → Bonding (one way) grows into attachment (two way) → Maladaptive signs and blues need teaching and referral

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Motherhood: pregnancy, acquaintance, new normal (first 4 months), maternal identity (around 4 months).
  2. Bonding is unidirectional (parent to infant). Attachment is bidirectional (parent and infant).
  3. Maternal touch: fingertips, whole hand, en face.
  4. Postpartum blues: hormones, stress, and fatigue. Teaching, family encouragement, referrals.
  5. Quiet alert is the best time for interacting. Deep sleep: do not wake or feed.

🎤 Transition to parenthood

Marked 🎤 = said in her Day 2 lecture. Where the lecture and slides differ, this guide uses the lecture.

TopicWhat she said
What shapes itAge (teen or older mom), experience, siblings or grandparents at home, family structure. Do not assume a mother of four knows everything. The teaching is just different.
Stages of motherhood1) Commitment and attachment, early preparation, in PREGNANCY. 2) Acquaintance with and attachment to the infant. 3) Moving toward a new normal (first 4 months or so). 4) Achievement of the maternal identity (around 4 months). It varies by history and relationships.
FathersAdaptation is more sudden. Shaped by his own father, his culture, and his partner's idea of a father. Praise his interactions, like a diaper change.
Teen parentsFewer life experiences and coping skills. May live with their parents. Financial and educational challenges. Grandparents may be more involved. Need more teaching: "Watch me this time, next time I watch you."
Same-sex parentsOften use artificial insemination or a donor. Support the co-parenting role. Use inclusive language. Assess your own feelings first.
BondingONE way: parent to infant. Cuddling, kissing the baby, breastfeeding.
AttachmentTWO way: the parent answers the cry, the baby responds to comfort, the parent knows the baby's cry from three rooms away. Reciprocal behaviors.
Maternal touchTentative fingertips, then stroking with the hand, then face to face with eye contact and holding close.
ContactBreastfeeding is contact. Encourage dads to do kangaroo care (skin to skin).
Risk for ineffective bondingNo interest in the baby, negative comments, ignoring cues (sitting across the room while the baby cries), anger or sadness, mood swings.
Infant statesSleep, drowsy, and crying all change how a baby communicates. She said she does not expect you to memorize those charts.
Family situationsMultipara: fatigue, worry about the other children accepting the baby. Sibling rivalry is normal. Let the sibling hold and touch the baby. Hearing loss: flick the lights before entering. Vision loss: announce yourself and do not move things.
Postpartum bluesA normal reaction to hormones, fatigue, and stress. Starts soon after birth and resolves in about 2 weeks. Anger, anxiety, sadness, weeping, trouble sleeping or eating. KEY: she can SAFELY care for her baby. Usually no medicine. Postpartum depression is next week.
🧠 Bonding vs attachment
Bonding = one way. Attachment = two way
Bonding: parent to baby (kiss, cuddle, breastfeed). Attachment: both respond to each other (the cry gets an answer).
🧠 Teaching a nervous parent
Watch me, then I watch you
Do it once yourself, then she does it while you stay beside her.
🧠 Blues vs depression
Blues: she can still care for the baby
About 2 weeks. Hormones, fatigue, stress. No safety problem.
🧠 Touch
Fingertips, hand, eyes
Fingertip touch, then stroking, then face to face.

🧪 Say it first: Parenthood and bonding

Say the answer out loud first. Then tap the question to check yourself.

When does motherhood begin?
In pregnancy (commitment, attachment, preparation).
Name the 4 stages of motherhood.
Pregnancy preparation; acquaintance and attachment; moving toward a new normal; maternal identity (about 4 months).

Bonding is one way (parent to infant). Attachment is two way (both).

Cuddling, kissing, breastfeeding.
Give 3 attachment behaviors.
Answering the cry, the infant responding to comfort, recognizing the baby's cry.

What does an EPDS score over 10 mean?

🪤 Traps to dodge

⚠️ Bonding vs attachmentBonding goes one way, parent to infant. Attachment goes both ways. Naming, kissing, and cuddling are bonding. Responding to cries and becoming cue sensitive are attachment.
⚠️ When motherhood startsThe first stage is in pregnancy, not at birth.
⚠️ Nurse self-checkWith same-sex parents the nurse must first self-assess her own feelings.
⚠️ Blues are not a diagnosis to ignoreTeach and encourage. Thoughts of harming self or the baby are a 911 sign.

📖 Definitions: parenthood, bonding, and blues (37 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Say each meaning out loud, then check.

TermMeaning
Transition to parenthoodA developmental process. Nursing actions support parental roles. It is affected by childhood experiences, support system, finances, and strength of the partnership. Fatigue and relationship stress are common.
Four stages of motherhood1) Commitment, attachment, and early preparation during pregnancy. 2) Acquaintance with and attachment to the infant. 3) Moving toward a new normal (first 4 months). 4) Achievement of maternal identity (around 4 months).
Commitment, attachment, and early preparationThe first stage of motherhood. It occurs during pregnancy (her slide question, answer A pregnancy).
Moving toward a new normalThe third stage of motherhood. It covers the first 4 months.
Achievement of maternal identityThe fourth stage of motherhood, at around 4 months.
Fatherhood adaptationDifferent and more sudden than motherhood. Affected by fatherhood models and culture and the partner's concept of a father. The nurse helps him process thoughts and feelings about the new role.
Adolescent parentsFewer life experiences and coping skills. The parenting style can be harsh. Mothers typically live with their parents.
Same-sex parentsAbout 5.1% of childbearing women identify as LGBT. There is a co-mothering role. The non-childbearing mother may feel stress from lack of support. Nurses must first self-assess their own feelings.
BondingUnidirectional emotional feelings from parent to infant. Examples: en face, calling the baby by name, cuddling the baby close, talking or singing to the baby, kissing, and breastfeeding or holding the baby close when bottle-feeding.
AttachmentBidirectional (two-way) feelings between parent and infant. Examples: parents respond to the infant's cry, the infant responds to the parents' comforting measures, parents stimulate and entertain the infant while awake, and parents become cue sensitive.
En faceFace-to-face eye contact between parent and infant. It is the third stage of maternal touch.
Cue sensitiveParents who notice and respond to the infant's behavior and signals. An attachment behavior.
Maternal touch stagesFirst: tentative fingertip touch. Second: strokes the baby's face using the whole hand. Third: en face, face-to-face eye contact.
Parent-infant contactFosters attachment and bonding. Breastfeeding is a form of contact, and paternal contact matters too.
Communication between parent and childA sensory experience. The infant communicates with coos, cries, facial expressions, and touch, which helps parents learn and react to the infant.
Maladaptive communicationNo interest in the baby, negative comments about the baby, ignoring the baby's cues and needs, anger or sadness at the baby or partner, and mood swings.
Risk factors for ineffective bondingListed on her slide as a topic under bonding and attachment. Maladaptive communication is the warning pattern to recognize.
Family dynamicsCo-parenting and concerns of single mothers, multiparas with fatigue and stress, sibling rivalry, parents with sensory or physical impairments, and social services and community health nurses as resources.
Postpartum bluesMild, short mood changes caused by hormones, stress, and fatigue. They resolve on their own in about 2 weeks, and the mother can still safely care for her baby (the key difference from depression). Signs: anger, anxiety, mood swings, sadness, weeping, and difficulty sleeping or eating. Nursing actions: teaching, family encouragement, and referrals.
Infant state: deep sleepMinimal body twitches and eye movement, cycles between deep and light sleep. Do not try to wake or feed the infant.
Infant state: light sleepMore active body movement and may smile. More easily aroused and stimulated.
Infant state: drowsyAwakens easily and can be rocked back to sleep or made more awake. May enjoy being held and cuddled, responds to gentle stimuli, and may self-comfort by sucking.
Infant state: quiet alertEyes open, quiet and attentive. The best time for interacting.
Infant state: active alertMore sensitive to stimuli with active body movement, and may be tired, hungry, or need changing. Decrease stimuli, provide a quiet environment and comfort measures.
Infant state: cryingGrimaces, cries, or whimpers. The infant may self-comfort. Meet the infant's needs.
Kangaroo careSkin to skin contact. Encourage fathers to do it too to build bonding and attachment.
Risk for ineffective bondingA nursing diagnosis used in care plans. A mother who is not interested in the baby, ignores cues, or sits across the room while the baby cries is a warning sign.
Teaching a fearful parentShow me first this time, then next time I watch you and stay with you. Especially helpful for teen parents.
Sibling rivalryThe older child may act out or grieve losing the baby role. This is normal. Reassure the parents and involve the sibling in holding and touching the baby.
Hearing loss accommodationFlick the lights on and off before entering the room, as a way of knocking.
Vision loss accommodationAnnounce yourself and do not move things around in the room.
Blues versus depressionThe key difference is that a mother with blues can safely care for her baby. Postpartum depression is covered next week.
EPDS score over 10The mother is at high risk for postpartum depression and should call her OB. She may need referrals, family support, or a mental health counselor.
Co-parenting role (same-sex parents)The nurse supports the shared parenting role, uses inclusive language, and assesses her own feelings first.
Artificial inseminationOften used by same-sex couples. They may choose a known or an unknown donor.
Bonding behaviorsCuddling, kissing the baby, and breastfeeding. They are one way, from parent to infant.
Attachment behaviorsThe parent answers the cry, the infant responds to comfort, and the parent knows the baby's cry from another room. They go both ways.

👩 Day 2: Maria Johnson Case Study

Her birthing experience case study, with the answers and discharge teaching.

🧠 The big idea

One patient, start to finish: Maria Johnson walks through labor, birth, recovery, and discharge.
Admission (is she in labor?) → Progression (variable decelerations) → Delivery (golden hour) → Recovery (firm vs boggy fundus) → Discharge teaching (7 questions)

🎤 Maria Johnson, what she taught along the way

Marked 🎤 = said in her Day 2 lecture. Where the lecture and slides differ, this guide uses the lecture.

TopicWhat she said
AdmissionG2P1 at 39 weeks 4 days. Contractions every 3 to 4 minutes lasting 45 to 60 seconds. 5 cm, 80% effaced, -1 station. First stage, active phase. Comfort: relaxation, deep breathing, epidural if she wants one.
Epidural window5 cm is a good time. A multipara at 8 to 9 cm may deliver in 20 to 30 minutes, so it can be too late. It cannot be placed once she is pushing.
3 hours laterStronger contractions, urge to push, membranes ruptured with clear fluid, very anxious. 8 cm, 100%, 0 station. Abrupt decreases in FHR with contractions.
The decelerationsIn lecture she called these "head compression." Abrupt decreases are variable decelerations from cord compression. Head compression is early decelerations, which are gradual. Know both.
Right after birthNewborn cried, good tone, skin to skin. Placenta complete. Nurse assesses the newborn and the cord, and Maria every 15 minutes: vitals, fundus, lochia, perineum.
At 45 minutesModerate blood on the pad, fundus firm and midline at the umbilicus, EBL 350 mL. Priorities: stable BP before she goes to the bathroom, rest, nutrition, hydration. One more 15 minute check, then every 30.
"Why do you push my belly?"To check that the uterus is firm so she does not hemorrhage.
Fundus to the right or leftThe bladder is probably full. Risk of atony.
Day 2 discharge questionsBleeding 5 to 6 weeks, red then pink then white. Urinate every 3 to 4 hours so there is no pressure on the uterus. Latch, cracked nipples, milk in 4 to 5 days. Pain should improve, not worsen. Infection signs: POST BIRTH. Activities and sex when cleared. Feeling sad or overwhelmed is normal. Follow-up: baby 1 to 2 days, mom at least 6 weeks, set before discharge.

Say the answer out loud first. Then tap the question to check yourself.

First stage, active phase.

Around 5 cm. Too late once she is pushing, or at 8 to 9 cm in a multipara.

Variable decelerations from cord compression (she said "head compression" in lecture).

To check the uterus is firm and prevent hemorrhage.

Every 3 to 4 hours.

About 4 to 5 days.

It should be getting better, not worse.

When do follow-up visits happen?
Baby within 1-2 days of discharge, Maria at least 6 weeks. Set before discharge.

❓ Her case questions with answers

QuestionAnswer
Which findings support that Maria is in labor?Regular contractions that are getting closer, with cervical change (5 cm, 80% effaced)
What do dilation, effacement, and station mean?Opening in cm, thinning in percent, and the position of the presenting part compared with the ischial spines (minus is above, plus is below)
What is the FHR pattern?Recurrent abrupt decreases with contractions: variable decelerations from cord compression. Reposition, assess, and tell the provider
"Why do you keep pushing on my belly?"To check that the uterus is firm, since a firm uterus controls bleeding
What does a boggy uterus suggest?Uterine atony and increased bleeding risk
Does Maria need Rho(D) immune globulin?No. She is O positive

🏠 Maria's discharge questions

She asksTeach her
How long will I bleed?Lochia: rubra, serosa, alba. 200 to 500 mL over 3 to 6 weeks
When should I urinate and why?Every 3 to 4 hours. A full bladder can displace the uterus and cause atony
What about breastfeeding and breast changes?Engorgement. Breastfeeding teaching, or cool compresses and cabbage leaves if not nursing
How much pain is normal?Mild soreness is expected. Take pain medicine as ordered. Report pain that is severe or not helped
How will I know I have an infection or complication?POST BIRTH: temperature 100.4 F or higher, pad soaked in an hour, leg that is red and warm, incision not healing, headache with vision changes. 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, seizures, thoughts of harm
When can I resume normal activities?Rest when the baby rests. Sex when lochia stops, perineum is healed, and she is ready, with contraception first
What if I feel persistently sad or overwhelmed?Tell the provider. Blues are common and short. EPDS before discharge and again at 10 days (over 10 means call the OB). Thoughts of harm mean 911

🧮 Maria's GTPAL

Before birth: G2 P1. After birth: G2 T2 P0 A0 L2 (two pregnancies, two term births, no preterm births, no abortions, two living children).

🩺 Think like a nurseWhen a case study ends with a patient's questions, answer each in plain words and tie it back to the list: lochia, bladder, breasts, pain, POST BIRTH, activity, mood.

🩺 Lecture vs slides, and what is still unconfirmed

  • Variable vs head compression: the slide pattern (abrupt decreases with contractions) is variable decelerations from cord compression. In lecture she said "head compression." If a question says "abrupt," choose cord compression. If it says "gradual" or "early," choose head compression.
  • Active phase at 5 cm: she called 5 cm active labor. Other sources say 6 cm. Use 5 cm for her exam.
  • Discharge timing: the case says discharged on postpartum day 2.

🧮 Day 2: Oxytocin Dosage Math

Her worked example, the four steps, two calculators, and practice problems. Definitions first.

🧠 The big idea

The hard part is keeping units straight, not the math.
Units to milliunits (x 1,000) → mU divided by mL = concentration → Ordered mU/min divided by concentration = mL/min → x 60 = mL/hr

She said this looks a lot scarier than it is. Most people go wrong by forgetting to convert hours, minutes, milliunits, or units.

⭐ Know these cold

  1. 1 unit = 1,000 milliunits (mU). 1 liter = 1,000 mL. 1 hour = 60 minutes.
  2. Concentration (mU/mL) = total mU in the bag divided by mL in the bag.
  3. Pump rate in mL/min = ordered mU/min divided by the concentration.
  4. Multiply mL/min by 60 to get mL/hr, because the pump runs in mL per hour.
  5. Check your answer backward: mL/hr divided by 60, times the concentration, should give the ordered mU/min.
🧠 Pump math
Thousand, Divide, Divide, Sixty
Times 1,000 (units to mU). Divide by mL (concentration). Divide the order by it (mL/min). Times 60 (mL/hr).

✏️ Her class problem, step by step

StepWorkAnswer
OrderOxytocin 0.5 mU/min. Bag: 5 units in 1 liter of lactated Ringer's. Set the pump in mL/hr.
1 Convert1 L = 1,000 mL. 5 units x 1,000 = 5,000 mU.5,000 mU in 1,000 mL
2 Concentration5,000 mU / 1,000 mL5 mU/mL
3 mL per minute0.5 mU/min / 5 mU/mL0.1 mL/min
4 mL per hour0.1 mL/min x 606 mL/hr

This is number 9 on her practice worksheet. In class a student first said 500 instead of 5,000 mU, which shows how easy the unit slip is.

🧰 Calculator: find the pump rate

Type the order and the bag. It shows every step so you can compare it with your own work.

🔁 Calculator: find the dose from the pump

Run it backward to check your work, or to find what a client is receiving.

🪤 Traps to dodge

⚠️ Units vs milliunitsThe order is in mU/min but the bag is in units. Convert the bag to mU first (x 1,000).
⚠️ Liters vs mLConvert 1 liter to 1,000 mL before dividing.
⚠️ Minutes vs hoursYour answer after dividing is mL per MINUTE. The pump needs mL per HOUR, so multiply by 60.
⚠️ Bag size changes the concentration5 units in 500 mL is twice as strong as 5 units in 1,000 mL. Always use the volume given.
⚠️ Decimal slipsIf your answer is 10 times too big or too small, a decimal moved. Check it backward.

📝 Practice problems (try, then tap)

Order 4 mU/min. Bag 10 units in 1,000 mL. mL/hr?
10 units = 10,000 mU. 10,000 / 1,000 = 10 mU/mL. 4 / 10 = 0.4 mL/min. x 60 = 24 mL/hr.
Order 6 mU/min. Bag 30 units in 500 mL. mL/hr?
30,000 mU / 500 mL = 60 mU/mL. 6 / 60 = 0.1 mL/min. x 60 = 6 mL/hr.
Order 3 mU/min. Bag 20 units in 1,000 mL. mL/hr?
20,000 / 1,000 = 20 mU/mL. 3 / 20 = 0.15 mL/min. x 60 = 9 mL/hr.
Order 2 mU/min. Bag 5 units in 500 mL. mL/hr?
5,000 / 500 = 10 mU/mL. 2 / 10 = 0.2 mL/min. x 60 = 12 mL/hr.
Order 1 mU/min. Bag 10 units in 500 mL. mL/hr?
10,000 / 500 = 20 mU/mL. 1 / 20 = 0.05 mL/min. x 60 = 3 mL/hr.
Pump at 18 mL/hr. Bag 10 units in 1,000 mL. mU/min?
10 mU/mL. 18 / 60 = 0.3 mL/min. x 10 = 3 mU/min.
Pump at 12 mL/hr. Bag 20 units in 1,000 mL. mU/min?
20 mU/mL. 12 / 60 = 0.2 mL/min. x 20 = 4 mU/min.
Pump at 6 mL/hr. Bag 5 units in 1 liter. mU/min?
5 mU/mL. 6 / 60 = 0.1 mL/min. x 5 = 0.5 mU/min (her class order).

📖 Definitions: oxytocin math (15 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Say each meaning out loud, then check.

TermMeaning
Milliunit (mU)One thousandth of a unit. 1 unit of oxytocin = 1,000 milliunits.
Oxytocin concentrationMilliunits in the bag divided by mL in the bag. 5 units in 1,000 mL = 5,000 mU in 1,000 mL = 5 mU/mL.
Oxytocin pump rate steps1) Convert units to milliunits. 2) Find the concentration in mU/mL. 3) Ordered mU/min divided by mU/mL gives mL/min. 4) Multiply by 60 for mL/hr.
Oxytocin class exampleOrdered 0.5 mU/min, bag 5 units in 1 liter. Concentration 5 mU/mL, 0.5 divided by 5 = 0.1 mL/min, times 60 = 6 mL/hr.
Oxytocin unit trapThe hardest part is keeping units straight: units vs milliunits, minutes vs hours, liters vs mL.
Desired dose (oxytocin)The ordered dose, such as 0.5 mU/min. This is what the client should get.
Available (oxytocin)What is in the bag, such as 5 units in 1,000 mL. Convert it to mU per mL.
Pump rate (mL/hr)The number the nurse programs into the pump. It equals mL/min times 60.
Checking backwardDivide mL/hr by 60 and multiply by mU/mL. The result should equal the ordered mU/min.
Units to milliunitsMultiply by 1,000.
1 liter in mL1,000 mL.
1 hour in minutes60 minutes.
mL/min to mL/hrMultiply by 60.
Concentration formulamU divided by mL.
Order divided by concentrationGives mL per minute.
🩺 Think like a nurseA pump rate is a high-alert number. Say the order, the bag, and your answer out loud, run it backward to check it, and have a second nurse verify before starting.

Question 1

A liter of Lactated Ringers is ordered to be infused at a rate of 70 mL/hr. How long will it take to infuse?

hr
min
Show worked solution
Time = volume / rate.
1,000 mL / 70 mL/hr = 14.2857 hr.
0.2857 hr x 60 = 17 min.
14 hours 17 minutes (about 14.3 hr).

Answer: 14 hr 17 min
Common slip: Divide the volume by the rate: 1,000 mL / 70 mL/hr. The decimal part of the hours is not minutes, so multiply it by 60.

Question 2

The newborn is ordered ampicillin 50 mg/kg. The infant weighs 3 kg. How many mg will you administer?

mg
Show worked solution
50 mg/kg x 3 kg = 150 mg.

Answer: 150 mg
Common slip: Multiply the dose per kg by the weight in kg.

Question 3

A postpartum woman is ordered ibuprofen 400 mg PO. Available: 200 mg tablets. How many tablets will you give?

tablets
Show worked solution
400 mg / 200 mg per tablet = 2 tablets.

Answer: 2 tablets
Common slip: Ordered divided by available.

Question 4

The provider orders betamethasone 12 mg IM. Available: 6 mg/mL vials. How many mL will you give?

mL
Show worked solution
12 mg / 6 mg per mL = 2 mL.

Answer: 2 mL
Common slip: Desired over have: 12 mg / 6 mg/mL.

Question 5

A patient is ordered 1000 mL of Lactated Ringers to be given over 12 hours. How should you set your flow rate in mL/hr on your pump?

mL/hr
Show worked solution
1,000 mL / 12 hr = 83.33, so 83 mL/hr.

Answer: 83 mL/hr
Common slip: Volume divided by hours: 1,000 / 12. Round to a whole number for the pump.

Question 6

A 55 kg patient is to receive a single IV dose of ondansetron 0.2 mg/kg for prevention of pregnancy induced nausea and vomiting. Ondansetron is available in a multi-dose vial (MDV) of 10 mg/5 mL. How many mL will you administer? (Round to the tenths)

mL
Show worked solution
Dose: 0.2 mg/kg x 55 kg = 11 mg.
Vial: 10 mg / 5 mL = 2 mg/mL.
11 mg / 2 mg per mL = 5.5 mL.

Answer: 5.5 mL
Common slip: Two steps: first the dose in mg (0.2 x 55), then the mL from the vial strength (10 mg per 5 mL is 2 mg per mL).

Question 7

Heparin 10,000 units in 100 mL is infusing at 13.9 mL/hr. How many units per hour are being given?

units/hr
Show worked solution
10,000 units / 100 mL = 100 units/mL.
100 units/mL x 13.9 mL/hr = 1,390 units/hr.

Answer: 1,390 units/hr
Common slip: Find units per mL first (10,000 / 100), then multiply by mL/hr.

Question 8

Calculate the fluid volume infused to the nearest mL. Infusion rate: 25 mL/hr for 2 hours and 30 mins.

mL
Show worked solution
2 hr 30 min = 2.5 hr.
25 mL/hr x 2.5 hr = 62.5 mL, which rounds to 63 mL.

Answer: 63 mL
Common slip: Change 2 hr 30 min to 2.5 hr, then multiply by the rate. 62.5 rounds up.

Question 9

Mr. Smith has 1000 mL of NS to infuse at 50 mL/hr. How long will it take to infuse? (Round to the nearest hour)

hr
Show worked solution
1,000 mL / 50 mL/hr = 20 hours.

Answer: 20 hours
Common slip: Volume divided by rate.

Question 10

The healthcare provider prescribes oxytocin (Pitocin) 0.5 milliunits/minute for a client in labor. One liter Ringer's Lactate with 5 units of oxytocin (Pitocin) is infusing. The nurse should program the infusion pump at how many mL/hr?

mL/hr
Show worked solution
5 units x 1,000 = 5,000 mU in 1,000 mL = 5 mU/mL.
0.5 mU/min / 5 mU/mL = 0.1 mL/min.
0.1 x 60 = 6 mL/hr.

Answer: 6 mL/hr
Common slip: If you got 0.1, that is mL per MINUTE. Multiply by 60 for mL per hour. This is the one she worked in class.

Question 11

Doctor orders 675 mL of 0.9% NS to infuse over 3 hours. With a tubing drop factor of 15 gtt/mL, how many drops per min should be given?

gtt/min
Show worked solution
3 hr x 60 = 180 min.
675 mL x 15 gtt/mL / 180 min = 10,125 / 180 = 56.25.
56 gtt/min.

Answer: 56 gtt/min
Common slip: Convert 3 hours to 180 minutes. Then volume x drop factor / minutes. Round to a whole drop.

Question 12

Order is for 50 mL to infuse over 50 min with a tubing drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. What will the infuse rate be in gtt/min? Round your answer to the whole number.

gtt/min
Show worked solution
50 mL x 15 gtt/mL / 50 min = 15 gtt/min.

Answer: 15 gtt/min
Common slip: Volume x drop factor / minutes. The minutes are already given.

Question 13

Doctor orders 500 mL of D5W with 20 units IV oxytocin. Begin at 1 mU/min and increase by 1 mU/min every 30 min as needed. Maximum dose is 11 mU/min. What is the IV rate in mL/h for the beginning infusion? Round answer to the tenths.

mL/hr
Show worked solution
20 units x 1,000 = 20,000 mU in 500 mL = 40 mU/mL.
1 mU/min / 40 mU/mL = 0.025 mL/min.
0.025 x 60 = 1.5 mL/hr.
Bonus: every 1 mU/min adds 1.5 mL/hr, so the maximum 11 mU/min is 16.5 mL/hr.

Answer: 1.5 mL/hr
Common slip: Units to mU first: 20 units = 20,000 mU. Then 20,000 / 500 = 40 mU/mL. Then 1 / 40 = 0.025 mL/min, and x 60.

Question 14

Calculate the pounds and ounces for a child that weighs 3000 g. (Round oz to the nearest whole number)

lb
oz
Show worked solution
3,000 g / 1,000 = 3 kg.
3 kg x 2.2 = 6.6 lb.
0.6 lb x 16 = 9.6 oz, which rounds to 10.
6 lb 10 oz.

Answer: 6 lb 10 oz
Common slip: Grams to kg (divide by 1,000), kg to lb (x 2.2), then the decimal pounds x 16 for ounces.

🔬 Diagnostics Drill

Unlimited practice: FHR strips, Bishop score, Edinburgh (EPDS), and the tests and procedures. Pick a level and go.

🔬 How to use this tab

Four drills, unlimited practice. Pick a level, work a strip, a cervix, a screening form, or a question, then read the reason. Your counts save on this device.

  1. FHR strips: a new tracing every tap. Read it in order: baseline, variability, decelerations, category, action.
  2. Bishop: score each factor, add them, decide if the cervix is ready.
  3. Edinburgh (EPDS): convert each answer to points (the reverse scoring is the trap), add, then act.
  4. Procedures quiz: NST, CST, BPP, AFI, nitrazine, ferning, Leopold, internal monitors, Coombs, and more.

Levels: Core = one clear feature. Hard = mixed findings and intermittent patterns. Max = exam traps (absent variability with decelerations, bradycardia with moderate variability, scores right at the cut-off).

📊 Read every strip in this order

StepAskNormal
1 BaselineAverage rate over 10 minutes, nearest 5, ignoring accelerations and decelerations110 to 160 bpm
2 VariabilityHow big is the wiggle from peak to trough?Moderate, 6 to 25 bpm
3 Accels and decelsWhich type? Recurrent (50% or more of contractions) or intermittent?Accelerations or early decelerations are fine
4 CategoryI, II, or IIII
5 ActionWhat do I do and who do I tell?Routine care for Category I
🧠 Say it like this
Baseline 140, moderate variability, recurrent late decelerations: Category II.
Use the standard words so the provider hears the same picture you see. Do not write reassuring or nonreassuring alone.
CategoryWhat it takes
IBaseline 110 to 160, moderate variability, no late, variable, or prolonged decelerations. Early decelerations and accelerations may be present.
IIIAbsent variability with recurrent late decelerations, recurrent variable decelerations, or bradycardia, OR a sinusoidal pattern.
IIEverything else. Tachycardia, bradycardia with variability, minimal or marked variability, any prolonged deceleration, and recurrent decelerations with some variability left.

Recurrent means with 50% or more of contractions. VEAL CHOP: Variable = Cord, Early = Head, Accel = OK, Late = Placenta.

🧮 Bishop score: what each factor earns

Factor0123
DilationClosed1 to 2 cm3 to 4 cm5 cm or more
Effacement0 to 30%40 to 50%60 to 70%80% or more
Station-3-2-1 or 0+1 or +2
ConsistencyFirmMediumSoftnone
PositionPosteriorMidpositionAnteriornone

Highest total is 13. 8 or more is favorable (induction is likely to work). 5 or less is unfavorable, so the cervix is ripened first with dinoprostone (Cervidil, Prepidil), misoprostol (Cytotec), or a Foley balloon. 6 to 7 sits in between. A modified Bishop score swaps cervical length for effacement.

📝 Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)

ItemScoring
Items 1, 2, 4Points go 0, 1, 2, 3 down the list of answers as printed
Items 3, 5 to 10Reverse scored: 3, 2, 1, 0 down the list
Total0 to 30. Her cut-off: above 10, call the OB
Item 10Any answer other than never (thoughts of self-harm) needs immediate safety action, whatever the total
WhenBefore discharge and again at home at about 10 days

It screens. It does not diagnose. The client fills it out herself, the nurse adds the points. Postpartum blues peak at about day 5 and fade by 2 weeks, so persistence and impaired function point away from blues.

🧪 Antepartum tests you can be asked about

TestWhat it showsReads as
NSTAccelerations with movement, noninvasiveReactive: 2 accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds within 20 minutes. Nonreactive: not met after 40 minutes
CSTHow the baby handles 3 contractions in 10 minutes (oxytocin or nipple stimulation)Negative (good): no late decelerations. Positive (bad): lates with 50% or more of contractions
BPPMovement 3+, tone 1+, breathing over 30 seconds, fluid pocket over 2 cm, reactive NST. 2 points each8 to 10 normal, 4 to 5 abnormal, under 2 chronic (worst)
AFIFour-quadrant fluid total5 to 25 cm normal. Under 5 oligohydramnios (cord compression). Over 25 polyhydramnios
NitrazineAlkaline fluid turns paper dark blue (pH 7 to 7.5)Yellow = acidic vagina. False blue from blood, semen, alkaline urine
FerningDried amniotic fluid crystallizes in a fern shapeFern pattern = amniotic fluid

Contraindications to a CST: placenta previa, prior classical cesarean, and risk for preterm labor.
