🧪 Procedure and test questions

📖 Vocabulary by chapter

420 terms. Tap a chapter to filter, then drill them in Flash Study Game or Match Games.

FHR Monitoring (21)

TermMeaning
Baseline FHRAverage fetal heart rate over 10 minutes, excluding accelerations and decelerations. Normal is 110 to 160 bpm.
Fetal tachycardiaBaseline above 160 bpm for 10 minutes or more.
Fetal bradycardiaBaseline below 110 bpm for 10 minutes or more.
VariabilityFluctuation in the baseline. Absent undetectable, minimal 5 or less, moderate 6 to 25 (normal), marked over 25.
AccelerationAbrupt rise of 15 bpm or more for 15 seconds or more. Reassuring.
Early decelerationGradual drop that mirrors the contraction. Caused by fetal head compression. Benign.
Variable decelerationAbrupt drop of 15 bpm or more lasting 15 seconds to under 2 minutes. Caused by umbilical cord compression.
Late decelerationGradual drop with the lowest point after the peak of the contraction. Caused by uteroplacental insufficiency. Ominous when recurrent.
Prolonged decelerationDrop of 15 bpm or more lasting 2 minutes or more but under 10 minutes.
Sinusoidal patternSmooth wave-like FHR pattern. Ominous. Category III.
TachysystoleMore than 5 contractions in 10 minutes averaged over 30 minutes.
Category INormal tracing: baseline 110 to 160, moderate variability, no late or variable decelerations.
Category IIIndeterminate tracing. Anything not Category I or III. Needs evaluation and surveillance.
Category IIIAbnormal tracing. Absent variability with recurrent late or variable decelerations or bradycardia, or sinusoidal. Immediate action.
Intrauterine resuscitationBedside measures to improve fetal oxygenation: reposition, stop oxytocin, IV bolus, oxygen, check for cord prolapse, notify the provider.
Leopold maneuversFour abdominal palpation steps to find fetal lie, presentation, and position, used to place the Doppler over the fetal back.
Tocodynamometer (toco)External belt device over the fundus that records contraction frequency and duration but not intensity. Also called: Toco.
IUPCIntrauterine pressure catheter. Measures contraction pressure in mm Hg. Requires ruptured membranes.
Fetal scalp electrodeInternal electrode that reads the FHR directly. Needs ruptured membranes, dilation, and an accessible presenting part. Also called: FSE, internal fetal monitor.
Chain of commandThe steps for escalating a safety concern when a provider does not respond: charge nurse, supervisor, then department chair.
VEAL CHOPVariable = Cord compression, Early = Head compression, Acceleration = OK, Late = Placental insufficiency.

Labor basics (39)

TermMeaning
Intrapartum periodThe period of labor. It begins with the onset of uterine contractions (UCs) and lasts until expulsion of the placenta. Also called: Labor.
Four stages of laborFirst: dilation and effacement. Second: expulsion of the fetus. Third: expulsion of the placenta. Fourth: recovery.
Labor triggers (maternal)Pressure on the cervix, hormones, and uterine contractions (UCs).
Labor triggers (fetal)The placenta, prostaglandins, and fetal cortisol.
Premonitory signsSigns of impending labor: Braxton-Hicks contractions, cervical changes, nesting, weight loss, low backache and sacroiliac discomfort, bloody show, and lightening.
True labor (Ch 13)Regular contractions that increase in frequency and intensity and change the cervix, causing effacement and dilation. Hydration or sedation does not stop them.
False laborContractions with no change in the cervix. Activity does not change the pattern, and hydration or sedation slows or stops them. Also called: Braxton-Hicks contractions.
Cervical changes (ripening)Softening and thinning of the cervix in the days before labor, getting it ready to efface and dilate. It also moves from a posterior toward an anterior position. A low Bishop score may call for a cervical ripening agent such as misoprostol (Cytotec).
Nesting (premonitory)A sudden burst of energy and an urge to clean and prepare the home shortly before labor.
Weight loss (premonitory)A small weight loss of about 1 to 3 lb in the days before labor, from fluid shifts and hormones.
Low backache and sacroiliac discomfortBack and pelvic joint pain before labor, as hormones relax the pelvic joints and the fetus presses down.
Five P's of laborPowers, Passage, Passenger, Psyche, Position.
PowersThe forces that move the fetus out: involuntary uterine contractions and voluntary pushing.
PassageThe maternal pelvis and birth canal. It includes the pelvic structure type.
PassengerThe fetus. Its skull, attitude, lie, presentation, and position all affect how it passes through.
PsycheThe woman's frame of mind: her culture, fear, anxiety, and support.
Position (fifth P)The relation of the fetal reference point to the mother's pelvis. Frequent maternal position changes also enhance comfort and promote optimal fetal positioning.
Contraction frequencyTime from the beginning of one contraction to the beginning of the next. Timed in minutes.
Contraction durationTime from the beginning of a contraction until its end. Timed in seconds.
Contraction intensityStrength of the contraction: mild (feels like the nose), moderate (chin), strong (forehead). Measured in mmHg with an intrauterine catheter.
Resting toneThe tension of the uterine muscle between contractions.
Palpation of contractionsFingertips on the fundus to feel contractions. Simple, but can be very inaccurate compared with an IUPC.
SROMSpontaneous rupture of membranes: the amniotic sac breaks on its own.
Nitrazine testNitrazine paper or a swab touched to vaginal fluid. Blue means amniotic fluid.
FerningA sample of vaginal fluid dried on a slide. A fern pattern under the microscope means amniotic fluid.
Bishop scoreA score that predicts how ready the cervix is for labor induction. It scores dilation, consistency, effacement, position, and station from 0 to 3 points each. A score of 8 or more for a client at term is favorable (ATI).
Go to the birthing facility whenMembranes rupture, intense pain, bloody show increases or frank bleeding, marked decrease or absence of fetal movement, or severe headache, vision changes, or strong epigastric pain.
Shared decision-makingIncluding the patient in developing her plan of care while respecting her culture, background, and preferences.
LighteningThe fetus descends into the true pelvis, about 2 weeks before labor in first-time mothers. It may not happen in later pregnancies. Breathing gets easier and urinary frequency increases.
Mucus plugThe mucus that seals the cervical canal during pregnancy. It is lost as the cervix changes, with increased vaginal discharge.
Bloody showPink or reddish discharge from small blood vessels breaking as the cervix softens. It is not the mucus plug itself. Frank bleeding (bright red blood) is different and needs to be reported.
When to go to the birthing facilityMembranes rupture, intense pain, bloody show increases or frank bleeding, marked decrease or absence of fetal movement, or severe headache, vision changes, or strong epigastric pain.
Powers (primary)The involuntary uterine contractions that dilate the cervix and push the fetus down. They start at the fundus and are rhythmic and intermittent.
Labor triggers (hormonal)Oxytocin, prostaglandins, estrogen, and cortisol.
Secondary powersVoluntary pushing by the mother during the second stage. The primary powers are the involuntary uterine contractions.
Estrogen and progesterone at termEstrogen rises and increases the uterus's ability to contract. Progesterone is withdrawn.
Fetal HPA axisThe baby's hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis. It raises cortisol, which causes an inflammatory response, releases prostaglandins, and leads to contractions.
Braxton Hicks contractions (lecture)Practice labor. Felt in the second and third trimester, like mild menstrual cramps. Mostly in the front of the abdomen, not consistent, and they ease with movement or a position change.

Passage and passenger (34)

TermMeaning
Cervical effacementThinning and shortening of the cervix. 0% is a canal 2 cm long, 50% is 1 cm long, and 100% means the canal is obliterated.
Cervical dilationOpening of the cervix, measured in centimeters from closed (0) to complete (10 cm).
StationThe relationship of the ischial spines to the presenting part of the fetus. It assesses fetal descent. Station 0 is at the ischial spines, minus is above, plus is below.
Cervical exam documentationWritten as dilation/effacement/station. For example, 3 cm, 50% effaced, minus 2 station is documented as 3/50/-2.
Closed/thick/highHow an unassessable cervix is documented: not dilated, not effaced, and the fetal head or station cannot be assessed.
Vaginal examA sterile exam of the cervix and presenting part. It checks dilation, effacement, station, and presenting part. Never done with unexplained vaginal bleeding until previa is ruled out.
Gynecoid pelvisThe classic female pelvis with a round inlet. The most favorable shape for vaginal birth.
Android pelvisThe male-type pelvis with a heart or wedge-shaped inlet that narrows toward the outlet. Often a difficult fit, but vaginal birth is still possible.
Anthropoid pelvisAn oval pelvis that is longer from front to back than side to side.
Platypelloid pelvisA flat pelvis that is wide side to side and short from front to back. The most difficult shape for vaginal birth and the least common (about 3% of women). Vaginal birth is usually not possible.
FontanelA soft spot where skull bones meet. It lets the skull mold. The anterior is diamond shaped and the posterior is triangular.
SutureA membrane-filled seam between fetal skull bones. Coronal, sagittal, lambdoidal, and frontal sutures let the bones overlap in labor.
MoldingThe shaping of the baby's skull as the bones overlap at the sutures to fit through the birth canal.
AttitudeThe posture of the fetus: the relationship of fetal parts to one another. Good attitude is flexion (chin to chest). Extension is the opposite.
Flexion (attitude)Chin tucked to chest and limbs folded in. The best attitude for passing through the pelvis.
LieThe relationship of the fetal spine to the maternal spine: longitudinal (parallel), transverse (perpendicular), or oblique (slanted).
Longitudinal lieThe fetal spine is parallel to the maternal spine. The normal lie, with the head or buttocks down.
Transverse lieThe fetal spine is perpendicular (across) the maternal spine. A vaginal birth is not possible, so a cesarean is needed.
PresentationThe fetal part that enters the pelvic canal first. Cephalic (head), breech (buttocks or feet), or shoulder.
Presenting partThe part of the fetus lying closest to the cervix, felt on vaginal exam.
Cephalic presentationThe head enters first. Most common, and includes vertex, brow, and face presentations.
Vertex presentationHead fully flexed with the occiput (back of the head) entering first. The most common and most favorable.
Brow presentationThe head is partly extended with the forehead first. It has the largest diameter (13.5 cm), so vaginal birth is usually not possible.
Face presentationThe head is fully extended with the face first. Smaller diameter (9.5 cm) than the brow.
Breech presentationThe buttocks or feet enter the pelvis first, instead of the head.
Frank breechHips flexed and knees extended, with the buttocks presenting first. The legs are up in front of the body.
Complete breechHips and knees both flexed, so the baby sits cross-legged with the buttocks presenting.
Footling breechOne or both feet present first, with the hips and knees extended. It carries the highest risk of cord prolapse.
Fetal positionThe relationship of a fetal reference point (occiput, chin, sacrum, or shoulder) to a quadrant of the mother's pelvis. The best position is the occiput anterior.
Occiput anteriorThe back of the fetal head faces the front of the maternal pelvis. The ideal position for labor. Also called: OA.
Leopold first maneuverDetermines which fetal part is in the fundus.
Leopold second maneuverDetermines the location of the fetal spine (back) versus the small parts.
Leopold third maneuverDetermines the fetal presenting part. The hand grasps just above the symphysis pubis.
Leopold fourth maneuverDetermines the cephalic prominence. The examiner faces the mother's feet.

Stages and birth (57)

TermMeaning
First stage of laborOnset of labor to complete cervical dilation (10 cm). It has a latent, an active, and a transition phase. It is the longest stage.
Latent phaseEarly labor, 0 to 5 cm. She is calm, talkative, and can follow directions. Contractions are irregular and mild to moderate, every 5 to 30 minutes lasting 30 to 45 seconds.
Active phase6 to 10 cm (it starts once she passes 5 cm). Contractions every 3 to 5 minutes lasting 40 to 90 seconds. More anxiety, apprehension, increased pain, nausea, and vomiting.
Transition phaseThe end of the active phase, about 8 to 10 cm. The most intense contractions. She may be irritable, nauseated, shaky, and feel rectal pressure.
Second stage of laborComplete dilation (10 cm) to birth of the baby. The expulsive stage, with maternal pushing.
Signs of the second stageAn intense need to push when the baby reaches the pelvic floor, burning from tissue stretching, bloody show increases, contractions intense and closer together, and the perineum flattens as the rectum and vagina bulge.
CrowningThe widest part of the fetal head is visible at the vaginal opening and does not go back between contractions.
Closed glottis pushingValsalva: pushing while holding the breath. No longer recommended.
Open glottis pushingPushing with sound (grunting or yelling) while breathing out. The recommended method.
Third stage of laborBirth of the baby to delivery of the placenta.
Signs of placental separationThe uterus becomes a ball shape, the cord lengthens, and there is a gush of blood.
Schultze mechanismThe placenta separates from the center first and delivers with the shiny fetal side first. Most common. Remember: Shiny Schultze.
Duncan mechanismThe placenta separates from the edge first and delivers with the rough maternal side first. Remember: Dirty Duncan.
Fourth stage of laborThe immediate postpartum recovery period, about the first 1 to 4 hours after the placenta delivers. Assess fundal height, bleeding, tone, and vital signs. Also called: Recovery.
EngagementThe fetal head passes through the pelvic inlet.
DescentMovement of the fetus down through the birth canal.
Flexion (cardinal movement)The chin moves to the chest when the head meets resistance from the maternal tissues.
Internal rotationThe fetal head turns to align with the long axis of the maternal pelvis.
ExtensionThe presenting part pivots under the pubic bone, which allows the head to be born.
External rotationAfter the head is born, the shoulders align with the anteroposterior diameter of the pelvis.
ExpulsionThe anterior shoulder is delivered, followed rapidly by the rest of the fetal body.
Cardinal movementsThe seven moves the fetus makes in labor, in order: engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, external rotation, expulsion.
EpisiotomyA surgical cut in the perineum to enlarge the vaginal opening. It can be midline (straight down) or mediolateral (to the side). It is done less often now because evidence shows little benefit.
Midline episiotomyAn incision straight down toward the anus. Easier to repair and less painful, but can extend to the anal sphincter.
Mediolateral episiotomyAn angled incision to the side. Less risk of tearing into the rectum, but more pain and harder to repair.
LacerationA tear of the cervix, vagina, or perineum during birth. The perineum is the most common site.
First degree lacerationInjury to the skin only.
Second degree lacerationSkin, mucous membranes, and the perineal body (muscles).
Third degree lacerationSkin, mucous membranes, and perineal muscles, extending into the anal sphincter.
Fourth degree lacerationExtends through the rectal mucosa and exposes the lumen of the rectum.
Laceration preventionWarm compresses, perineal massage, and perineal stretching.
Quantitative blood lossMeasuring blood loss by volume or weight. About 500 mL is usual. 1000 mL is hemorrhage.
Postpartum hemorrhage preventionMassage the fundus and empty the bladder, and give a uterotonic.
UterotonicsDrugs that make the uterus contract to prevent or treat postpartum bleeding: oxytocin (Pitocin), methylergonovine (Methergine), carboprost (Hemabate), misoprostol (Cytotec).
Oxytocin (Pitocin)IV high alert drug, titrated. Stimulates uterine smooth muscle to produce intermittent contractions. Used for labor induction and control of bleeding after the placenta is born.
Methylergonovine (Methergine)Increases the tone, rate, and amplitude of contractions, reducing blood loss. Prevents or treats postpartum hemorrhage, uterine atony, and subinvolution. A second line drug. Avoid in hypertension.
Carboprost tromethamine (Hemabate)Given IM into a large muscle or the uterus. Increases contractions to manage postpartum bleeding from uterine atony. A second line option, and used for patients with hypertension. Avoid in asthma.
Misoprostol (Cytotec)Given orally, sublingually, buccally, or rectally. A second line uterotonic for postpartum bleeding. Not given vaginally during hemorrhage.
Golden hourThe first 60 minutes after birth. A transition for the neonate and new family. If physiologically safe, the infant stays on the birthing parent's chest. Newborn-family attachment time.
Apgar scoreA newborn score at 1 minute and 5 minutes. Scores heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex activity, and color, 0 to 2 each (maximum 10).
Apgar heart rate2 = above 100 bpm. 1 = slow, below 100 bpm. 0 = absent.
Apgar respiratory effort2 = good cry. 1 = slow, irregular. 0 = absent.
Apgar muscle tone2 = active motion. 1 = some flexion of extremities. 0 = flaccid.
Apgar reflex activity2 = vigorous cry. 1 = grimace. 0 = none.
Apgar color2 = completely pink. 1 = body pink, blue extremities. 0 = pale or blue.
Normal newborn values (Apgar guide)Heart rate 100 to 160 bpm, respiratory rate 30 to 60, muscle tone flexed, reflex activity cry, color body pink.
Culturally sensitive carePatient-centered care that asks about and integrates the woman's cultural and religious values, beliefs, and practices into her labor care.
Placental delivery windowThe placenta should deliver within 30 minutes of the birth of the baby.
Apgar interpretation10 is a perfect score. 8 to 9 is safe. 7 and under needs monitoring. Below 4 needs resuscitation right away. A low 1 minute score that improves by 5 minutes is usually okay.
Central cyanosisBlue color of the trunk, lips, and tongue from low oxygen. A concern at any time. Blue hands and feet alone (acrocyanosis) are a different, milder finding.
Epidural and the second stageAn epidural can lengthen the second stage of labor.
AcrocyanosisBlue hands and feet in a newborn. Normal and common, especially in the first 24 hours, and scores 1 for color. Different from central cyanosis (face, mouth, nose), which is a concern.
Retained placentaA placenta that has not delivered within 30 minutes of birth. The client is at risk for postpartum hemorrhage.
Perineal care after birthIce for the first 24 hours only, since longer can impair healing. Dermoplast spray, witch hazel pads, and ibuprofen for cramps help.
Laceration prevention (before birth)Warm compresses, perineal massage, and stretching. Never put warm compresses on tissue that is already torn.
Carboprost side effectsNausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Contraindicated in asthma because it can cause bronchospasm.
Methylergonovine mechanismAn ergot alkaloid that contracts the uterus and constricts blood vessels, so it is contraindicated in hypertension.

Pain relief and medications (30)

TermMeaning
Gate control theory of painTwo different nerve fibers have gates at various levels. Overstimulating one gate (touch, pressure, heat) prevents the pain impulse from entering or traveling.
EffleurageLight strokes in a circular motion with the palm of the hand, usually on the abdomen.
CounterpressureSteady firm pressure on the sacrum to relieve back pain in labor.
Nonpharmacologic pain measuresRelaxation and breathing, counterpressure, massage and effleurage, guided imagery, distraction and focal points, hydrotherapy, warm and cold packs, and positioning.
HydrotherapyUsing warm water, such as a shower or tub, to ease labor discomfort.
AnalgesiaReduces the perception of pain without loss of consciousness. Opioids and nitrous oxide are examples.
AnesthesiaLoss of sensation. It may be local, regional, or general.
Opioid analgesics in laborMorphine, butorphanol (Stadol), nalbuphine (Nubain), and fentanyl (Sublimaze). Given IM or IV. Early in labor only.
Butorphanol (Stadol)An opioid agonist-antagonist analgesic given IM or IV in labor.
Nalbuphine (Nubain)An opioid agonist-antagonist analgesic given IM or IV in labor.
Fentanyl (Sublimaze)A fast acting opioid analgesic used in labor, IV or in epidural and spinal blocks. Sufentanil is used the same way.
Nitrous oxideAn inhaled gas that decreases the perception of pain. Self-administered by mask during contractions.
Naloxone (Narcan)The opioid reversal drug. Keep it available when giving opioids because the newborn may have respiratory depression.
Neonatal respiratory depressionThe main risk when opioids are given too close to delivery, because they cross the placenta.
Local anesthesiaNumbs one small area. Lidocaine is used for episiotomy and laceration repair.
Regional anesthesiaBlocks a larger area: pudendal block, epidural block, and spinal block.
General anesthesiaThe whole body is unconscious. Used for emergency cesarean sections.
Pudendal blockA transvaginal injection near the pudendal nerve that numbs the perineum for the second stage and delivery.
Epidural blockAnesthetic injected into the epidural space, outside the dura. A catheter stays in so doses can be repeated. Fentanyl or sufentanil may be added.
Spinal blockAnesthetic injected into the subarachnoid space (with spinal fluid). Fast, a single dose, mainly for cesarean birth.
Contraindications to regional anesthesiaHistory of spinal surgery or abnormalities, coagulation defects, and hypovolemia.
Epidural nursing considerationsNausea and vomiting are common. Respiratory depression and hypotension are the biggest concerns. Maternal hypotension can cause fetal distress. Avoid the supine position.
Basic principle of labor pain reliefRelief with minimal risk to mother and baby. Opioid use disorder may need higher doses.
SufentanilAn opioid given in epidural and spinal (regional) blocks, like fentanyl.
Anesthesia safety stepsKnow the type of anesthesia being used, get consent, and complete a time out before the procedure.
Opioid use disorder and labor painA client with opioid use disorder may need higher doses of pain medication.
Epidural timing and effectsUsually placed around 5 cm in the lumbar epidural space. It can lengthen the second stage and raise the chance of vacuum or forceps delivery and oxytocin augmentation. About 70% of women in the US receive one.
Informed consent for an epiduralThe provider explains the procedure. The nurse witnesses the signature only if the client understands it. If she does not, the nurse does not sign.
Time outA pause before the procedure to verify the right client by name and birth date, and the right procedure.
Nonpharmacologic measures (lecture list)Relaxation and breathing, massage, counterpressure, hydrotherapy, warm and cold packs, guided imagery, and positioning.

FHR monitoring (Ch 13 deck additions) (26)

TermMeaning
AWHONN (FHR)Association of Women's Health, Obstetric and Neonatal Nurses. It publishes the recommendations for FHR monitoring.
Goal of EFMInterpret and continually assess fetal condition and start appropriate interventions based on the tracing. EFM = electronic fetal monitoring.
External FHR monitoringMonitor applied to the maternal abdomen where the fetal back lies. Continuous or intermittent. Uses two transducers: one on the fetal back and one over the fundus for contractions.
Internal FHR monitoringA spiral electrode on the fetal scalp, which requires ruptured membranes and a cervix dilated at least 2 cm. Gives a more accurate rate. Avoid with placenta previa, herpes, or HIV.
Doppler deviceHandheld ultrasound used for intermittent FHR monitoring.
Baseline tracing timeRecord a baseline for 20 minutes when starting monitoring. Intermittent timing depends on labor stage and risk factors.
Episodic changesFHR changes not associated with uterine contractions.
Periodic changesFHR changes associated with uterine contractions.
Goals of intrauterine resuscitationMaximum uterine blood flow, umbilical circulation, and maternal-fetal oxygenation.
Autonomic control of the FHRThe parasympathetic nervous system (vagus) slows the rate. The sympathetic nervous system speeds it up.
BaroreceptorsPressure sensors that slow the fetal heart rate when blood pressure rises, such as during cord compression.
ChemoreceptorsSensors that react to low oxygen or high carbon dioxide and raise the fetal heart rate and blood pressure.
TerbutalineA tocolytic that stops contractions. Used for tachysystole with a non-reassuring tracing.
Monitoring multiple gestationEach fetus needs its own transducer. Before the membranes rupture, two external transducers (baby A and baby B). After rupture, one external and one internal.
Preterm fetus and FHRTolerates little stress. Baseline is a bit higher but still in the normal range. Variable decelerations are the most common pattern, even without contractions. Late and prolonged decelerations are still concerning.
Uterine activity measuresKnow frequency, duration, intensity, resting tone, and tachysystole.
Tachysystole nursing actionTreat the cause even when the tracing is normal: stop oxytocin, remove a cervical ripening agent, or give a tocolytic such as terbutaline.
Checking FHR after rupture of membranesAssess the fetal heart rate right away to look for cord prolapse.
Baseline (lecture definition)A consistent rate for at least 2 minutes within a 10 minute window, not counting accelerations or decelerations.
Variability levelsAbsent: flat line. Minimal: 5 bpm or less. Moderate: 6 to 25 bpm, the ideal. Marked: over 25 bpm.
Category shortcutLearn Category I (normal) and Category III (always abnormal). Everything else is Category II (indeterminate).
Variable deceleration managementReposition the mother and check for a prolapsed cord.
Tachycardia causesFever, infection, dehydration, anxiety, anemia, certain medications or drugs such as cocaine, compensation for hypoxia, and fetal cardiac problems.
Bradycardia causesMother lying on her back, hypotension, dehydration, placental abruption, electrolyte imbalance, cord occlusion, and cardiac problems.
Magnesium sulfate and FHRCauses CNS depression, which lowers FHR variability.
Things that skew the contraction tracingBreathing, pushing, vomiting, and fetal movement (sharp spikes). Reposition the transducer if the tracing looks obscure or inverted.

Day 2: Assessment, uterus, lochia, perineum (51)

TermMeaning
Maternal mortalityDeath from complications of pregnancy or childbirth up to 1 year after birth.
Maternal mortality rateMaternal deaths per 100,000 births. Slide figures for 2023: 12.5 per 100,000 at 25 years or younger, 18.1 at ages 25 to 39, 59.8 at 40 years or older.
Healthy People 2030The national set of health goals named on her slide for preventing maternal death.
Leading causes of maternal death (slide pie chart)Obstetric hemorrhage 44%, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy 28%, pregnancy-related infections 10%, abortive outcomes 7%, other obstetric causes 7%, anesthetic complications 2%.
Postpartum periodThe first 6 weeks after childbirth. It includes physical changes plus social and emotional adaptation. Also called: Puerperium.
Postpartum assessment (overview)Vital signs, pain, breath and heart sounds, laboratory findings, and vaccination status, then breasts, uterus, bladder, bowel, lochia, episiotomy or lacerations or perineum or hemorrhoids, lower extremities, and emotions, bonding with the infant, fatigue, and psychosocial factors.
BUBBLE LEPostpartum head-to-toe memory aid: Breasts, Uterus, Bladder, Bowel, Lochia, Episiotomy (perineum), Lower extremities, Emotions. Also called: BUBBLE EE.
Uterine involutionThe return of the uterus to its nonpregnant state after birth. The nurse assesses the position, tone, and location of the fundus. The fundus is at the umbilicus after birth and drops about 1 fingerbreadth (1 cm) per day until it cannot be felt at about 9 days.
FundusThe top of the uterus. After birth it is assessed for position, tone, and location (height compared with the umbilicus).
Fundal assessment steps (slide)Instruct her to void first, then support the lower uterine segment while assessing the fundus.
Supporting the lower uterine segmentOne hand supports the lower uterus just above the symphysis pubis while the other hand assesses the fundus. Her slide lists it as a step of fundal assessment.
Firm fundusA well contracted uterus that feels like a firm ball. Expected after birth. Case study: firm, midline, at the level of the umbilicus.
Boggy uterusA soft, relaxed uterus. It most strongly suggests uterine atony and an increased risk of bleeding (case study question).
Uterine atonyFailure of the uterus to contract firmly after birth, leaving it boggy. It is on her Box 16.1 list of risk factors for postpartum hemorrhage.
SubinvolutionIncomplete involution of the uterus after birth.
Causes of subinvolutionRetained placental fragments, distended bladder, uterine myoma, and infection.
Complications of subinvolutionHemorrhage, pelvic peritonitis, salpingitis, and abscess formation.
Endometrial changesAssessed by examining the lochia. The appearance and amount of lochia show the progress of endometrial shedding and regeneration.
LochiaThe vaginal discharge after birth as the uterus sheds its lining. Total volume is about 200 to 500 mL and it can last 3 to 6 weeks. Lochia can last up to 5 weeks (patient education slide).
Lochia rubraDark red blood from the birth until 3 to 4 days postpartum. Flow like a heavy menstrual period, may have small clots, and the odor is fleshy like menstrual blood.
Lochia serosaPinkish-brownish discharge from about 4 to 12 days postpartum (about 2 weeks). The flow is a moderate to small amount.
Lochia albaYellowish-white discharge from about 12 days to 3 weeks postpartum. Scant, creamy, and whitish, gradually disappearing.
Lochia that goes backwardLochia should not progress backward. A return to rubra after serosa or alba needs a call to the OB because of hemorrhage risk. Her slide adds that overactivity or stress may cause it.
Scant lochiaBlood only on the tissue when wiped, or a stain on the peri pad less than 1 inch (2.5 cm).
Light lochiaA stain on the peri pad less than 4 inches (10 cm).
Moderate lochiaA stain on the peri pad less than 6 inches (15.2 cm).
Heavy lochiaA peri pad saturated within 1 hour.
REEDAScale for assessing perineum healing: Redness, Edema, Ecchymosis, Discharge or Drainage, Approximation.
Redness (REEDA)Erythema at the perineal repair or episiotomy site.
Edema (REEDA)Swelling of the perineal tissue.
Ecchymosis (REEDA)Bruising of the perineal tissue.
Discharge or drainage (REEDA)Fluid draining from the perineal wound. The nurse notes the amount and type.
Approximation (REEDA)How well the edges of the repair line up and stay together.
Reproductive system nursing focusUterine involution (position, tone, location of the fundus), the endometrium (lochia color, amount, odor), the vagina and perineum (REEDA), and breast care and assessment.
Postpartum vital sign schedule (lecture)Every 15 minutes right after delivery, every 30 minutes after about an hour, then every 4 hours for the first 24 hours. It is unit specific, and sicker clients are checked more often.
Postpartum labs (lecture)CBC to see how much blood was lost, rubella status to decide on MMR, and Rh status to decide on RhoGAM.
Tdap postpartum (lecture)Make sure the tetanus shot is current. It is mainly for pertussis (whooping cough), to protect the baby. Flu and COVID vaccines are also recommended.
Fundal progression (lecture)At the umbilicus on the day of delivery, then down about 1 fingerbreadth (1 cm) per day for about 9 days, until it cannot be felt.
Fundus not descendingA fundus that is not descending, or is coming back up, raises worry about incomplete involution (subinvolution).
Deviated fundus (lecture)A fundus displaced to the right or left means a full bladder is pressing on it. A full bladder can cause uterine atony. Have her void, and straight cath only if needed.
Uterine inversionThe uterus turns inside out. Supporting the lower uterine segment with one hand below and one on top during fundal assessment helps prevent it.
Retained placenta (lecture)A cause of subinvolution. The retained pieces must be removed.
Lochia gush on standingBlood pools while lying down and gushes out when she stands. This is normal. A constant trickle is not.
Fishy lochia odorWorry about infection. Normal lochia has a fleshy odor like menstrual blood.
Nulliparous cervix (picture A)The cervical os of a woman who has never had a baby is a small pinpoint.
Parous cervix (picture B)After childbirth the os becomes a slit-like opening.
Perineum check with every fundal checkWhenever the fundus is assessed, also look at the perineum to watch the repair and the bleeding.
Lower extremity assessmentLooks for blood clots (DVT). Clotting factors are high in pregnancy and take about 2 weeks to return to normal.
Obstetric hemorrhageThe number one cause of postpartum complications and maternal death. Hypertensive disorders come second.
Abortive outcomesMiscarriage and induced abortion. Listed among the causes of pregnancy-related death.
Fundus displaced right or leftSuggests a full bladder pushing the uterus aside. Have her void before judging the fundus.

Day 2: Breasts and body systems (56)

TermMeaning
Breast care and assessmentAssess the breasts and teach breastfeeding and non-breastfeeding patients how to care for them.
EngorgementSwollen, inflamed, painful breasts with lactation. The infant has difficulty grasping the nipple, which can disrupt breastfeeding (Figure 15.4).
Suppressing lactationMilk stops eventually when there is no stimulus (no infant suckling or pumping). Cool compresses (15 minutes on, 15 minutes off per her lecture) and cold cabbage leaves ease engorgement.
Cool compresses for engorgementApplied 15 minutes on and 15 minutes off (her lecture) to ease engorgement in a woman who is not breastfeeding.
Cold cabbage leavesA comfort measure for engorgement listed on her slide for suppressing lactation.
Percent who do not breastfeedAround 30% of mothers will not breastfeed.
Estimated blood loss (EBL)Average 200 to 500 mL after a vaginal birth.
Orthostatic hypotensionA drop in blood pressure when she sits or stands up. She is at risk right after birth.
Expected postpartum labsH&H (hemoglobin and hematocrit) low and WBCs high.
Postpartum vital signsBP decreases slightly, RR decreases, temperature increases slightly, and there is an immediate weight loss.
Slight temperature rise (first 24 hours)A slight elevation in temperature during the first 24 hours postpartum is considered normal (her slide question, answer true).
Respiratory system postpartumReturns to the pre-pregnancy state by the end of the postpartum period. Breath sounds are assessed after birth.
Risk factors for pulmonary edemaOxytocin, large amounts of IV fluids, tocolytics, multiple birth, infection or preeclampsia, and bedrest.
Immune system postpartumSuppressed during pregnancy and returns to normal in the postpartum period.
Postpartum rubella vaccinationGiven to a woman who is rubella-nonimmune. She must prevent pregnancy for 4 weeks after the immunization.
Rho(D) immune globulinGiven to an Rh-negative woman who gave birth to an Rh-positive baby, when she is Coombs negative. Prevents Rh isoimmunization. Brand name: RhoGAM.
Rh isoimmunizationThe mother forming antibodies against Rh-positive blood. Prevented with Rho(D) immune globulin.
Coombs negativeHer antibody screen shows no Rh antibodies yet, so Rho(D) immune globulin can still prevent them.
Urinary risks postpartumBladder distention, urinary incontinence, an increased risk of UTI, and cystitis.
Urinary nursing actionsEncourage voiding every 3 to 4 hours and assess the volume excreted and for retention.
Fluid shiftFluid moves from the extravascular to the intravascular space after birth, about 6 to 8 liters.
Postpartum diuresisExcess pregnancy sodium and fluid are removed through inhibited aldosterone, angiotensin II, and vasopressin. Diuresis occurs during the first 2 weeks postpartum, with urine output up to 3000 mL/day.
Endocrine changes after birthAfter the placenta is delivered, estrogen, progesterone, and prolactin levels decrease. In breastfeeding women, prolactin increases in response to infant suckling.
DiaphoresisHeavy sweating after birth. It is an expected endocrine change.
Insulin sensitivity postpartumReturns in days, or in weeks if the woman is obese.
Return of menses10 to 12 weeks in nonlactating women. 4 to 5 months, and as much as 24 months, in lactating mothers.
Ovulation without mensesOvulation can occur before the first period returns, so she can become pregnant before she sees a period.
Diastasis recti abdominisSeparation of the rectus abdominis muscles along the linea alba. The nurse assesses for it in the muscular system.
Muscular and nervous nursing actionsAssess for diastasis recti abdominis, relieve muscle soreness, assess for return of sensation, headache, and fatigue, promote rest and sleep, and perform nursing actions.
Kegel exercisesSqueeze and lift the pelvic floor muscles (as if stopping urine or gas), hold 5 seconds, relax 5 seconds, repeat 5 times. They strengthen the pelvic floor.
Gastrointestinal changes postpartumConstipation, hemorrhoids, increased appetite, and weight loss. Encourage fluids and food.
Letdown reflexThe release of milk triggered by oxytocin. Infant suckling causes prolactin and oxytocin release.
Milk production hormonesAfter the placenta is delivered, estrogen and progesterone fall. Prolactin makes the milk and oxytocin causes letdown. Suckling is a positive feedback loop: more suckling, more milk.
ColostrumThe thick first milk. Mature creamy milk comes in about 4 to 5 days after delivery.
Breastfeeding on demandFeed whenever the baby acts hungry, about 8 to 12 times in 24 hours. Start each feeding on the breast offered last time.
Breastfeeding hand hygieneWash hands before breastfeeding to help prevent infection. ATI likes to ask about it.
Bra for a breastfeeding motherA well-fitted bra with no underwire. Underwire can cause clogged milk ducts.
Cracked nipples careCheck the latch for a deep latch, use lanolin cream, and express breast milk onto the nipples and let it dry.
Engorgement care when breastfeedingFrequent emptying, warm shower or warm compress before feeding, and cold between or after feedings. Never use cold before feeding because too much cold can dry up the milk supply.
Bra for a mother who is not breastfeedingA well-fitted supportive bra for the first 72 hours, and no breast stimulation, including warm showers running over the breasts.
Early ambulationVaginal birth clients are usually up within a couple of hours. Cesarean birth clients are up in about 12 to 24 hours, per facility policy.
SCDs and leg careSequential compression devices on while she is not up, and do not cross the legs. This keeps blood moving and prevents clots.
Excessive hypotension or tachycardia (postpartum)Worry about excessive blood loss and shock. A slightly low BP alone is expected.
Chills after birthWith a normal temperature, give a warm blanket. Fever with chills raises worry about infection, so notify the provider.
Meds that raise pulmonary edema riskOxytocin, terbutaline, and magnesium sulfate, along with large IV fluid volumes, preeclampsia, and bedrest.
Why Rh isoimmunization mattersThe mother makes antibodies against the baby's Rh-positive blood, which can put future pregnancies in jeopardy.
Stress incontinence postpartumLeaking urine with pressure. Epidural anesthesia, large fluid volumes, and urethral edema make voiding harder. Pelvic floor physical therapy helps if it lasts.
Diastasis recti courseUsually resolves on its own in about 6 to 8 weeks. If it does not, physical therapy or surgery may be needed.
Constipation causes postpartumDecreased GI motility from progesterone, less activity, dehydration or fluid loss, and fear of a bowel movement from lacerations or hemorrhoids. Give stool softeners, fiber, and fluids.
Hemorrhoid comfort measuresTucks pads and sitz baths. They usually resolve slowly on their own but can stay painful.
Postpartum weight lossAbout 11 to 12 lb at delivery (baby, blood, fluid), then about 5 to 8 lb more from diuresis. Most women are at pre-pregnancy weight by about 6 months.
Gestational diabetes postpartumInsulin needs drop significantly. If it was only gestational diabetes, she usually does not need insulin after birth.
Orthostatic hypotension (postpartum)A drop in blood pressure on standing. Risk after birth from blood loss. Check BP, sit her on the side of the bed to dangle, then help her stand.
DiuresisIncreased urine output after birth from falling estrogen. Up to about 3,000 mL a day, mostly in the first 12 hours, and uncommonly for up to 2 weeks.
First postpartum cycleOften without ovulation, but she can still ovulate. Menses return in about 10 to 12 weeks if not breastfeeding.
LanolinA breast cream used for cracked, sore nipples.

Day 2: Nursing management and discharge (38)

TermMeaning
Nursing management in the postpartum periodCulturally optimal care, promoting comfort, assisting with elimination, promoting activity, rest, and exercise, assisting with self-care, ensuring safety, counseling about sexuality and contraception, promoting nutrition, supporting the choice of newborn feeding method, teaching about breast care, and teaching about postpartum blues.
Postpartum follow-up visitA comprehensive assessment and depression screening within 4 to 6 weeks. Many women do not have postpartum follow-up.
Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)The screening tool for postpartum depression. Done before discharge, again at about 10 days at home, and at the follow-up visit. A score over 10 means call the OB.
Discharge teaching topicsNutrition and fluids, physical activity and exercise, rest and comfort, sexual activity, family planning and contraception, smoking cessation and relapse prevention, and warning signs.
Nonlactating calorie goal1,800 to 2,200 kcal per day.
Lactating calorie goalIncrease calories by about 450 to 500 kcal per day.
Postpartum dietA well-balanced diet high in protein for tissue repair. Iron supplementation may be required.
Prenatal vitamins postpartumRecommended until 6 weeks postpartum.
Activity and rest teachingKegel exercises, rest for healing and lactation, rest when the baby rests, and take medications as ordered (iron, vitamins, pain medications).
Resuming sexual activityDiscuss with the provider. General guideline: when lochia stops, the perineum is healed, and she is physically and emotionally ready.
Contraception before sexHave contraception in place before sex resumes. Breastfeeding is NOT contraception.
Smoking cessation teachingEncourage women who quit during pregnancy to continue to abstain, warn about secondhand smoke, and know that most who quit will relapse after delivery.
Risk factors for postpartum infectionOperative procedure (cesarean, vacuum), history of diabetes including gestational diabetes, prolonged labor over 24 hours, indwelling urinary catheter, anemia (hemoglobin under 10.5), multiple vaginal exams, prolonged rupture of membranes over 24 hours, manual extraction of placenta, and compromised immune system (HIV positive).
Risk factors for postpartum hemorrhagePrecipitous labor (under 3 hours), uterine atony, placenta previa or abruptio placentae, labor induction or augmentation, operative procedures, retained placental fragments, prolonged third stage (over 30 minutes), multiparity with more than three closely spaced births, and uterine overdistention (large infant, twins, hydramnios).
Precipitous labor (Box 16.1)Labor of less than 3 hours. A risk factor for postpartum hemorrhage.
Prolonged labor (Box 16.1)Labor of more than 24 hours. A risk factor for postpartum infection.
Prolonged third stage (Box 16.1)A third stage of labor of more than 30 minutes. A risk factor for postpartum hemorrhage.
Uterine overdistentionOverstretching of the uterus by a large infant, twins, or hydramnios. A risk factor for postpartum hemorrhage.
AWHONN POST BIRTHThe 2018 AWHONN discharge teaching project that tells women when to call 911 and when to call the provider.
Call 911 (POST BIRTH)Pain in the chest, obstructed breathing or shortness of breath, seizures, and thoughts of hurting yourself or the baby.
Call the provider (POST BIRTH, M-GILL)Bleeding that soaks through one pad per hour or a clot the size of an egg, an incision that is not healing, a red or swollen leg that is warm or painful to the touch, a temperature of 100.4 F or higher, and a headache that does not improve with medication or comes with vision changes.
Ice to the perineumIce for about the first 24 hours only. Longer than 24 hours can delay healing.
Perineal comfort productsDermoplast spray, Tucks pads, and witch hazel. Heat from a heating pad can also be used for comfort.
First-line postpartum pain medicinesIbuprofen (Motrin, Advil) and acetaminophen (Tylenol) first. Stronger options such as hydrocodone and acetaminophen (Norco) are for severe lacerations, hemorrhoids, or cesarean birth.
Safe first ambulationCheck BP, sit her on the side of the bed to dangle, then help her stand and walk with her. Never let her walk alone the first times because of orthostatic hypotension.
EPDS schedule (lecture)Before discharge, then a second copy at about 10 days postpartum at home. A score over 10 means call the OB.
Postpartum follow-up (lecture)Set the appointments before discharge. Newborn follow-up within 1 to 2 days of discharge. Mother at least 6 weeks. Many keep the pediatrician visit and skip the OB visit.
Contraception while breastfeedingBreastfeeding is unreliable. Avoid combined (estrogen) oral contraceptives. Progestin-only options are preferred: the mini pill, Depo-Provera injection, and an IUD, which is easy to place postpartum.
Combined oral contraceptivesPills with estrogen and progestin. Avoided while breastfeeding.
POST (call 911)Pain in the chest, Obstructed breathing or shortness of breath, Seizures, Thoughts of hurting yourself or the baby.
M-GILL (call the provider)Massive bleeding (pad an hour or egg-size clot), Growing incision problem, Infection (temperature 100.4 F or higher), Leg pain or swelling, Lingering headache or vision changes.
Temperature concern (lecture)A slight rise in the first 24 hours can come from dehydration or fluid loss. Worry if it comes with chills or continues past the first 24 hours.
Secondhand smoke riskChildren exposed are at higher risk of SIDS. Teach it because most who quit during pregnancy relapse after delivery.
Mini pillA progestin-only birth control pill (norethindrone). Preferred over combined pills while breastfeeding.
Depo-ProveraA progestin injection (medroxyprogesterone). An option for the breastfeeding mother.
IUD postpartumAn intrauterine device. It is easier to place postpartum and has no estrogen.
Rest with the babyTeach her to rest when the baby sleeps so she can heal and her milk can come in.
Pain medicine teachingPain medicine helps her do more of her usual activity, so encourage her to take it as ordered.

Day 2: Parenthood, bonding, and blues (37)

TermMeaning
Transition to parenthoodA developmental process. Nursing actions support parental roles. It is affected by childhood experiences, support system, finances, and strength of the partnership. Fatigue and relationship stress are common.
Four stages of motherhood1) Commitment, attachment, and early preparation during pregnancy. 2) Acquaintance with and attachment to the infant. 3) Moving toward a new normal (first 4 months). 4) Achievement of maternal identity (around 4 months).
Commitment, attachment, and early preparationThe first stage of motherhood. It occurs during pregnancy (her slide question, answer A pregnancy).
Moving toward a new normalThe third stage of motherhood. It covers the first 4 months.
Achievement of maternal identityThe fourth stage of motherhood, at around 4 months.
Fatherhood adaptationDifferent and more sudden than motherhood. Affected by fatherhood models and culture and the partner's concept of a father. The nurse helps him process thoughts and feelings about the new role.
Adolescent parentsFewer life experiences and coping skills. The parenting style can be harsh. Mothers typically live with their parents.
Same-sex parentsAbout 5.1% of childbearing women identify as LGBT. There is a co-mothering role. The non-childbearing mother may feel stress from lack of support. Nurses must first self-assess their own feelings.
BondingUnidirectional emotional feelings from parent to infant. Examples: en face, calling the baby by name, cuddling the baby close, talking or singing to the baby, kissing, and breastfeeding or holding the baby close when bottle-feeding.
AttachmentBidirectional (two-way) feelings between parent and infant. Examples: parents respond to the infant's cry, the infant responds to the parents' comforting measures, parents stimulate and entertain the infant while awake, and parents become cue sensitive.
En faceFace-to-face eye contact between parent and infant. It is the third stage of maternal touch.
Cue sensitiveParents who notice and respond to the infant's behavior and signals. An attachment behavior.
Maternal touch stagesFirst: tentative fingertip touch. Second: strokes the baby's face using the whole hand. Third: en face, face-to-face eye contact.
Parent-infant contactFosters attachment and bonding. Breastfeeding is a form of contact, and paternal contact matters too.
Communication between parent and childA sensory experience. The infant communicates with coos, cries, facial expressions, and touch, which helps parents learn and react to the infant.
Maladaptive communicationNo interest in the baby, negative comments about the baby, ignoring the baby's cues and needs, anger or sadness at the baby or partner, and mood swings.
Risk factors for ineffective bondingListed on her slide as a topic under bonding and attachment. Maladaptive communication is the warning pattern to recognize.
Family dynamicsCo-parenting and concerns of single mothers, multiparas with fatigue and stress, sibling rivalry, parents with sensory or physical impairments, and social services and community health nurses as resources.
Postpartum bluesMild, short mood changes caused by hormones, stress, and fatigue. They resolve on their own in about 2 weeks, and the mother can still safely care for her baby (the key difference from depression). Signs: anger, anxiety, mood swings, sadness, weeping, and difficulty sleeping or eating. Nursing actions: teaching, family encouragement, and referrals.
Infant state: deep sleepMinimal body twitches and eye movement, cycles between deep and light sleep. Do not try to wake or feed the infant.
Infant state: light sleepMore active body movement and may smile. More easily aroused and stimulated.
Infant state: drowsyAwakens easily and can be rocked back to sleep or made more awake. May enjoy being held and cuddled, responds to gentle stimuli, and may self-comfort by sucking.
Infant state: quiet alertEyes open, quiet and attentive. The best time for interacting.
Infant state: active alertMore sensitive to stimuli with active body movement, and may be tired, hungry, or need changing. Decrease stimuli, provide a quiet environment and comfort measures.
Infant state: cryingGrimaces, cries, or whimpers. The infant may self-comfort. Meet the infant's needs.
Kangaroo careSkin to skin contact. Encourage fathers to do it too to build bonding and attachment.
Risk for ineffective bondingA nursing diagnosis used in care plans. A mother who is not interested in the baby, ignores cues, or sits across the room while the baby cries is a warning sign.
Teaching a fearful parentShow me first this time, then next time I watch you and stay with you. Especially helpful for teen parents.
Sibling rivalryThe older child may act out or grieve losing the baby role. This is normal. Reassure the parents and involve the sibling in holding and touching the baby.
Hearing loss accommodationFlick the lights on and off before entering the room, as a way of knocking.
Vision loss accommodationAnnounce yourself and do not move things around in the room.
Blues versus depressionThe key difference is that a mother with blues can safely care for her baby. Postpartum depression is covered next week.
EPDS score over 10The mother is at high risk for postpartum depression and should call her OB. She may need referrals, family support, or a mental health counselor.
Co-parenting role (same-sex parents)The nurse supports the shared parenting role, uses inclusive language, and assesses her own feelings first.
Artificial inseminationOften used by same-sex couples. They may choose a known or an unknown donor.
Bonding behaviorsCuddling, kissing the baby, and breastfeeding. They are one way, from parent to infant.
Attachment behaviorsThe parent answers the cry, the infant responds to comfort, and the parent knows the baby's cry from another room. They go both ways.

Day 2: Maria Johnson case study (16)

TermMeaning
Maria Johnson (case study)A 28-year-old G2P1 at 39 weeks 4 days with regular contractions and pelvic pressure. Previous uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Prenatal course uncomplicated, GBS negative, membranes intact, no known drug allergies, blood type O positive.
G2P1Gravida 2 (second pregnancy, counting this one) and para 1 (one prior birth after 20 weeks). After Maria delivers she is G2P2, or T2 P0 A0 L2 in GTPAL.
Cervical dilation, effacement, and station (Maria)At admission 5 cm dilated, 80% effaced, -1 station. Three hours later 8 cm, 100% effaced, 0 station.
Recurrent abrupt decreases with contractionsThe FHR pattern in the labor progression table. This describes variable decelerations (cord compression), not a pattern to ignore.
EBL 350 mLMaria's blood loss at delivery. Within the usual 200 to 500 mL range for a vaginal birth.
Immediate post-birth findings (Maria)Uterus firm near the umbilicus, small amount of lochia rubra, mild perineal swelling, BP 118/74, HR 92.
Pushing on the belly (fundal checks)Why the nurse repeatedly checks the fundus: to confirm the uterus stays firm and to watch for atony and bleeding.
Maria's discharge questionsHow long will I bleed, when to urinate and why, breastfeeding and breast changes, how much pain is normal, signs of infection, when to resume activities, and what to do if persistently sad or overwhelmed.
Maria's GTPAL after birthG2 T2 P0 A0 L2.
Maria's EBL350 mL, within the usual 200 to 500 mL range.
Maria's admission cervix5 cm dilated, 80% effaced, -1 station.
Maria's cervix at 8 cm8 cm dilated, 100% effaced, 0 station.
Maria's blood typeO positive, so she does not need Rho(D) immune globulin.
Maria's FHR patternVariable decelerations from cord compression.
Maria's fundus at 45 minutesFirm, midline, at the level of the umbilicus.
Epidural windowThe time when an epidural can still be placed. 5 cm is a good time. It is too late once she is pushing.

Day 2: Oxytocin dosage math (15)

TermMeaning
Milliunit (mU)One thousandth of a unit. 1 unit of oxytocin = 1,000 milliunits.
Oxytocin concentrationMilliunits in the bag divided by mL in the bag. 5 units in 1,000 mL = 5,000 mU in 1,000 mL = 5 mU/mL.
Oxytocin pump rate steps1) Convert units to milliunits. 2) Find the concentration in mU/mL. 3) Ordered mU/min divided by mU/mL gives mL/min. 4) Multiply by 60 for mL/hr.
Oxytocin class exampleOrdered 0.5 mU/min, bag 5 units in 1 liter. Concentration 5 mU/mL, 0.5 divided by 5 = 0.1 mL/min, times 60 = 6 mL/hr.
Oxytocin unit trapThe hardest part is keeping units straight: units vs milliunits, minutes vs hours, liters vs mL.
Desired dose (oxytocin)The ordered dose, such as 0.5 mU/min. This is what the client should get.
Available (oxytocin)What is in the bag, such as 5 units in 1,000 mL. Convert it to mU per mL.
Pump rate (mL/hr)The number the nurse programs into the pump. It equals mL/min times 60.
Checking backwardDivide mL/hr by 60 and multiply by mU/mL. The result should equal the ordered mU/min.
Units to milliunitsMultiply by 1,000.
1 liter in mL1,000 mL.
1 hour in minutes60 minutes.
mL/min to mL/hrMultiply by 60.
Concentration formulamU divided by mL.
Order divided by concentrationGives mL per minute.

💓 FHR Monitoring

How to monitor the fetal heart rate properly, read the tracing, and act. Your instructor stressed this, and it is also where nurses face the most legal risk.

⚖️ Why this matters

The fetal heart rate is how you see fetal oxygenation.
Misreading or not acting on a tracing delays care
→ injury to the baby and claims against nurses and providers. Nurses are legally responsible for fetal monitoring and assessment.

  • Use standard NICHD terms so everyone describes the tracing the same way.
  • Clinical judgment: recognize the cue, analyze it, prioritize, act, and evaluate. Then report with SBAR and use the chain of command if no one responds.
  • Evidence-based practice sets how often you assess and what you do for each pattern.

🩺 Methods of monitoring

MethodHowNotes
Intermittent auscultationFetoscope or handheld Doppler over the fetal back. Listen for 30 to 60 seconds after a contractionUsed for low-risk labor. Count the rate, note rhythm, and the response to a contraction
External electronic monitoringUltrasound (Doppler) transducer for FHR and a tocodynamometer ("toco") over the fundus for contractions, held by beltsNoninvasive. The toco shows frequency and duration of contractions, not intensity
Internal electronic monitoringFetal scalp electrode for FHR and an intrauterine pressure catheter (IUPC) for contractionsNeeds ruptured membranes, enough cervical dilation (about 2 to 3 cm), and an accessible presenting part. More accurate. Invasive
🔍 Go deeper: Contraction assessment
  • Frequency: from the start of one contraction to the start of the next.
  • Duration: from the start to the end of the same contraction.
  • Intensity by palpation: mild feels like the tip of the nose, moderate like the chin, strong like the forehead. An IUPC measures pressure in mm Hg.
  • Resting tone: the uterus should relax and be soft between contractions.
  • Tachysystole: more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes, averaged over 30 minutes.

✅ Step by step: monitoring properly

  1. Explain the procedure, wash hands, and get consent. Place her in a comfortable position, not flat on her back (left side, semi-Fowler, or sitting)
  2. Do Leopold maneuvers to find the fetal back. Heart tones are loudest over the fetal back (for a vertex baby, the lower quadrant of the abdomen)
  3. Place the Doppler over the fetal back and the toco at the fundus. Secure the belts and recheck often
  4. Check the maternal pulse to be sure you are recording the baby and not the mother (a rate of 70 to 90 may be maternal)
  5. Assess contractions: frequency, duration, resting tone, and intensity
  6. Look at a 10 minute window. Identify baseline, variability, accelerations, and decelerations and how they relate to contractions
  7. Label it as Category I, II, or III
  8. Act on the category. Start intrauterine resuscitation for a nonreassuring pattern and call with SBAR
  9. Document on time, in standard terms, with what you did and who you told

⏱️ How often to assess

RiskActive first stageSecond stage (pushing)
Low riskEvery 30 minutesEvery 15 minutes
High risk or oxytocinEvery 15 minutesEvery 5 minutes

These are the commonly taught intervals (ACOG and AWHONN). Always follow your facility protocol and your instructor's version for exams. Reassess after any change: rupture of membranes, medication, epidural, change in contractions, or a change in her condition.

📏 Terms and normal values (NICHD)

TermDefinition
BaselineAverage rate over 10 minutes, rounded to 5 bpm, excluding accelerations and decelerations. Normal 110 to 160 bpm
TachycardiaBaseline above 160 bpm for 10 minutes or more
BradycardiaBaseline below 110 bpm for 10 minutes or more
VariabilityFluctuation in baseline. Absent: undetectable. Minimal: 5 bpm or less. Moderate (normal): 6 to 25 bpm. Marked: more than 25 bpm
AccelerationAbrupt rise of 15 bpm or more lasting 15 seconds or more (under 32 weeks: 10 bpm for 10 seconds). Reassuring
Prolonged acceleration2 minutes or more but under 10 minutes
Prolonged decelerationDrop of 15 bpm or more lasting 2 minutes or more but under 10 minutes
Sinusoidal patternSmooth wave-like pattern. Ominous

📉 Decelerations: cause and nursing action

🧠 Memory hook
VEAL CHOP
Variable = Cord compression. Early = Head compression. Acceleration = OK. Late = Placental insufficiency.
PatternWhat it looks likeCauseNursing action
EarlyGradual drop and return. A mirror image of the contraction. Lowest point matches the peak of the contractionFetal head compressionBenign. Continue to monitor. No intervention needed
VariableAbrupt drop (under 30 seconds to the low point) of 15 bpm or more, lasting 15 seconds to under 2 minutes. Shape and timing vary (V, U, or W)Umbilical cord compressionChange maternal position (side to side), stop oxytocin, check for cord prolapse by vaginal exam, give oxygen and IV fluid, notify provider. Amnioinfusion may be ordered
LateGradual drop that begins after the contraction starts, and the lowest point comes after the peak. Returns after the contraction endsUteroplacental insufficiency (poor oxygen to the fetus)Turn her to the left side, give IV fluid and oxygen, stop oxytocin, check her BP, notify provider now, prepare for possible urgent birth. Recurrent late decelerations are ominous
ProlongedDrop lasting 2 minutes or more but under 10 minutesCord prolapse, uterine hyperstimulation, maternal hypotension (supine or after an epidural), rapid descent, maternal seizureFind and fix the cause. Reposition, fluids, oxygen, stop oxytocin, check for prolapse, notify provider
AccelerationAbrupt rise of 15 bpm or more for 15 seconds or moreFetal movement or stimulation. A sign of a well-oxygenated fetusReassuring. Document it
Minimal or absent variabilityFlat line patternFetal sleep (usually under 40 minutes), opioids, magnesium sulfate, acidemiaLook for the cause. Stimulate the fetus. Absent variability with decelerations is serious

🚦 NICHD three-tier system

CategoryFindingsMeaning and action
I (normal)Baseline 110 to 160, moderate variability, no late or variable decelerations. Early decelerations and accelerations may be present or absentNormal acid-base status. Routine care and routine monitoring
II (indeterminate)Everything that is not Category I or III. Examples: tachycardia, bradycardia without absent variability, minimal or marked variability, recurrent variable decelerations, prolonged decelerationsNeeds evaluation, continued surveillance, and often resuscitation measures. Notify provider
III (abnormal)Absent variability with recurrent late decelerations, recurrent variable decelerations, or bradycardia, or a sinusoidal patternAbnormal acid-base status. Immediate action: resuscitation measures, notify provider, prepare for prompt birth

🩹 Intrauterine resuscitation (for a nonreassuring pattern)

Do these together, quickly, and tell the provider. Follow your facility protocol.

  1. Reposition her to the left side (or right, hands and knees) to improve blood flow
  2. Stop or reduce oxytocin if infusing, especially with tachysystole
  3. Give an IV fluid bolus (isotonic)
  4. Give oxygen by nonrebreather mask at about 10 L/min as protocol directs
  5. Do a vaginal exam to rule out cord prolapse and check dilation
  6. Check her vital signs and treat hypotension
  7. Notify the provider with SBAR. The provider may order a tocolytic (such as terbutaline) for tachysystole or amnioinfusion for variable decelerations
  8. Prepare for operative or assisted birth if the tracing does not improve

📞 SBAR for an abnormal tracing

PartExample
Situation"This is the nurse for Ms. J in room 4, 39 weeks, in active labor. She has recurrent late decelerations for the last 20 minutes."
Background"G2 P1, oxytocin at 12 milliunits per minute, epidural placed an hour ago, no allergies."
Assessment"Baseline 150 with minimal variability. Late decelerations with every contraction. BP 92/50, contractions every 2 minutes. I turned her left, started a fluid bolus, gave oxygen, and stopped the oxytocin."
Recommendation"I need you to come to the bedside now and evaluate for birth. Do you want me to prepare for a cesarean?"

📝 Documentation and legal protection

  • Chart the baseline, variability, accelerations, type of decelerations, contraction pattern, category, interventions, her and the baby's response, who you notified, the time, and the provider's response.
  • Use standard terms. Do not write "reassuring" or "nonreassuring" alone. Describe what you see.
  • Label and keep the strip. Never alter or erase an entry. Late entries are labeled as late.
  • If the provider does not respond to a concerning tracing, use the chain of command (charge nurse, then supervisor, then chair) and document that you did.
  • Patient safety comes before convenience.

🧪 Before labor: NST and biophysical profile

  • Nonstress test (NST): from 32 weeks for high-risk pregnancies. She eats first and lies on her left side. External monitor, event marker for movements, 20 to 30 minutes. Reactive: at least two accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds within 20 minutes. Nonreactive: not met after 40 minutes. More than half are false positives, so repeat, use vibroacoustic stimulation, or do a BPP.
BPP component2 points if
Body movements3 or more
Fetal tone1 or more flexion and extension
Fetal breathing1 or more lasting over 30 seconds
Amniotic fluid1 pocket over 2 cm
NSTReactive

Score 8 to 10 normal, 4 to 5 abnormal, under 2 chronic (the worst). Amniocentesis, CVS, and the other antepartum tests are in your Week 1 guide.

📎 Added from your Ch 13 and 14 deck

TopicWhat the slides say

📝 From your notes: FHR monitoring

TopicYour notes say
MonitoringAssess fetal position. External and internal monitoring. Changes in the placenta change the fetal heart rate
BaselineNormal 110 to 160 bpm. Tachycardia is above 160 for 10 minutes or more. Bradycardia is below 110 for 10 minutes or more
Memory aidVEAL CHOP MINE
CategoriesKnow the categories of fetal heart tracing interpretation. CATEGORY 3 IS ALWAYS BAD
Vocabulary to knowBaseline, variability, episodic and periodic
TerbutalineStops contractions

🎤 From the lecture: monitoring and strips

TopicHer lecture says
GoalAssess fetal condition and start the right intervention. AWHONN has the recommendations. FHR monitoring is a highly litigated area
External monitoringTwo transducers: one on the fetal back (find it with Leopold maneuvers) and one over the fundus for contractions. If the tracing is erratic, reposition the transducers first
Internal monitoringA scalp electrode screwed into the fetal head, plus an intrauterine pressure catheter (mmHg). Used when external monitoring is inadequate. Needs ruptured membranes and at least 2 cm dilation. Avoid with placenta previa, herpes, HIV
Reading the stripTop tracing is the FHR. Bottom is contractions. Big boxes are 1 minute and small boxes are 10 seconds. A baseline strip is 20 minutes. Intermittent monitoring depends on stage and risk. Doppler is common at home and birth center births
What affects the FHRThe placental unit. Parasympathetic (vagus) slows it. Sympathetic speeds it and gives variability, and is stimulated by hypoxia. Baroreceptors and chemoreceptors in the aortic arch. The CNS. Hormones (epinephrine, norepinephrine, vasopressin)

🎤 From the lecture: FHR vocabulary and categories

TermHer lecture says
BaselineA consistent reading for at least 2 minutes within a 10 minute window. Do not count accelerations or decelerations. Normal 110 to 160. Tachycardia above 160 for 10 minutes or more. Bradycardia below 110 for 10 minutes or more
Absent variabilityFlat line. Not a good sign
Minimal variability5 bpm or less. The baby may be sleeping, so stimulate or reposition
Moderate variability6 to 25 bpm. Ideal
Marked variabilityOver 25 bpm. The baby is irritated and something may be wrong
Episodic and periodicEpisodic is not tied to contractions. Periodic is tied to contractions
Category INormal. Baseline 110 to 160, moderate variability, accelerations present or absent, early decelerations present or absent, no variable or late decelerations
Category IIIndeterminate. Tachycardia, or bradycardia without absent variability, minimal or absent variability without recurrent decelerations, marked variability, prolonged decelerations over 2 minutes and under 10, or no accelerations after stimulation. Could be fine, could be bad
Category IIIAlways abnormal. Sinusoidal pattern, or absent variability with recurrent late or variable decelerations or bradycardia
Her tipLearn Category I and Category III. Everything else falls in the middle

🎤 From the lecture: causes and decelerations

FindingHer lecture says
Tachycardia causesFever, infection, dehydration, anxiety, anemia, medications or drugs such as cocaine, compensation for hypoxia, cardiac problems
Bradycardia causesMother on her back, hypotension, dehydration, placental abruption, electrolyte imbalance, cord occlusion, cardiac problems. Usually not a good sign
AccelerationAbrupt rise from baseline. Good, especially with contractions. No intervention
Early decelerationStarts before the peak, mirrors the contraction, head compression. No intervention, or identify labor progress
Variable decelerationAbrupt drop not tied to the middle of the contraction. Cord compression. Reposition the mother and check for a prolapsed cord
Late decelerationGradual drop after the peak of the contraction. Placental insufficiency. Turn off Pitocin, give oxygen, reposition, hydrate. If prolonged, cesarean
SinusoidalVery ominous. Needs a cesarean right away
VEAL CHOP MINEVEAL is the pattern, CHOP is the cause, MINE is the management
Intrauterine resuscitationReposition to free the cord. IV bolus of at least 500 mL. Oxygen at 10 L/min. Decrease oxytocin. Terbutaline to relax the uterus. The goal is blood flow to the uterus and placenta and good oxygenation for mom and baby

🎤 From the lecture: uterine activity and special cases

TopicHer lecture says
Frequency and durationFrequency is counted over 10 minutes, start to start, in minutes. Duration is start to end, in seconds
Intensity and resting toneIntensity is measured by palpation or internally in mmHg. Resting tone is the pressure between contractions, by internal monitoring or palpation
TachysystoleMore than 5 contractions in 10 minutes averaged over 30 minutes. Can cause fetal hypoxia. Treat regardless of fetal status by treating the cause: stop oxytocin, remove a cervical ripener such as misoprostol, or give a tocolytic
What skews the contraction tracingBreathing, pushing, vomiting, and fetal movement (sharp spikes). Baseline shifts with position changes. Reposition the transducer if the tracing is obscure or inverted
Preterm fetusTolerates stress poorly. Baseline a bit higher but still in the normal range. Variable decelerations are more common, even without contractions. Late and prolonged decelerations are still concerning. Magnesium sulfate lowers variability (CNS depression). Terbutaline or tachysystole can cause tachycardia in mother and fetus
MultiplesBefore rupture of membranes, two external transducers (baby A and baby B). After rupture, one external and one internal

🚦 Priority Decoder

Four clients, one nurse. This is the table that ranks them.

The ranking rule

Do not rank by how abnormal something sounds. Rank by Maslow first: physiological needs before safety and security, then belonging, esteem, and self-actualization. In other words, rank by how fast it can hurt the mother or fetus. Life-threatening bleeding, no fetal movement, and imminent danger come first. An acute change beats a stable abnormal finding. Routine labs and teaching come last.

  • Minutes: heavy bleeding with pain, cord or fetal distress, severe preeclampsia signs, imminent abuse, supine hypotension.
  • Hours: fever with urinary symptoms, decreased fetal movement, dehydration, possible DVT.
  • Days to weeks: routine screening, teaching, expected discomforts.
